posts.title: Google Summer of Code 2026 With the Kotlin Foundation: Recap
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Google Summer of Code 2026 has wrapped up! This was the Kotlin Foundation’s fourth year participating in GSoC, bringing new contributors into the Kotlin open-source ecosystem through hands-on projects and mentorship.
This year, two projects successfully reached completion, tackling two areas of the ecosystem: improving recursion support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend and building a global picture of where Kotlin is taught.
Congratulations to Ayako Hayasaka and Mark Seif Khalil, and a huge thank-you to our mentors for supporting them throughout the program!
Here’s more on what they accomplished.
Tail call support in the Kotlin/Wasm backend
Contributor: Ayako Hayasaka
Mentor: Charlie Zhang (JetBrains)
Ayako’s project added support for WebAssembly tail-call instructions to the Kotlin/Wasm backend. The compiler can now detect calls in tail position and emit return_call or return_call_ref, helping recursive Kotlin/Wasm programs avoid increasing the call stack.
In Ayako’s benchmarks, several recursive patterns became 1.7–4.3x faster at a recursion depth of 10,000. At a depth of one million, the same programs crashed without tail calls and completed successfully with them.
Testing the change on real-world projects also revealed an unexpected performance regression in V8. Ayako traced it to a missing optimization for return_call, submitted a fix, and had the patch merged into V8.
    
“What surprised me the most was that Ayako, after implementing the new WebAssembly instructions and using them in the Kotlin backend, actually found a bug in the Google V8 engine. Not only did she report the bug, she fixed it as well.”

            
Charlie Zhang
                                                        
Ayako has continued working on follow-up optimizations and other approaches to supporting recursive code beyond the original GSoC project.
For Ayako, GSoC 2026 was also a chance to work much more closely on language and runtime internals than in her everyday work.
“In my day job, I rarely get to touch the internals of a language, so I simply had a lot of fun with this opportunity. While investigating the slowdown, I had to read not only the compiler but also V8, and I realized how much there is to learn beyond the code I usually work on.”

            
Ayako Hayasaka
                                                        
Read Ayako’s full story → Final project report
Mapping the global Kotlin education landscape
Contributor: Mark Seif Khalil
Mentors: Ksenia Shneyveys (JetBrains) and Elizaveta Artser (JetBrains)
Mark’s project set out to create a structured overview of where and in what context Kotlin is being taught, considering that the information is spread across websites, course curricula, repositories, learning platforms, and other sources. The project brought that fragmented information together and created a structured and automated way to gather this data.
Over the course of GSoC 2026, Mark explored different sources and approaches to collecting this information, built a database, and developed a process for parsing and structuring data from multiple sources. 
“The biggest thing I learned is when to stop pushing on something that is not working and change my approach. This is a lesson I will keep with me in every project.”

            
Mark Seif Khalil
                                                        
The resulting project gives us a reusable foundation for monitoring Kotlin’s presence in education and identifying trends and gaps.
“What impressed us both the most about Mark was his ability to take an initially exploratory idea and bring his own vision for the research while continuously incorporating our feedback. Mark turned this scattered information into a resource we can actually use to understand Kotlin education worldwide.”

            
Ksenia Shneyveys, Elizaveta Artser
                                                        
Read Mark’s full story → Kotlin Education Landscape
Watch Mark’s GSoC reflection
Interested in contributing to Kotlin through a future Google Summer of Code – or mentoring a project yourself?
Join the #gsoc channel in the Kotlin Slack to meet the community, ask questions, and follow future GSoC announcements.

posts.title: IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin for Cursor and VS Code Hits 1.0
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Ten weeks ago, we opened up a preview of an LSP-powered extension that brings IntelliJ IDEA’s smartness for Java and Kotlin into VS Code and Cursor. As mentioned in that blog post, this is part of a bigger initiative: moving our JVM intelligence to wherever our users are, no matter what editor or agent they are using.
Today, we’re proud to announce 1.0, the first stable release of Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA.
And we’re not shipping it alone. This release is also the result of a close collaboration with the team at Cursor, who have worked alongside us to make Java and Kotlin a first-class experience in their development environment. 






Get Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from Visual Studio Marketplace
Get Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from Open VSX Registry
Why this matters
Agentic development is changing how software gets built. As agents take on more implementation work, developers spend less time manually editing code – and when they do edit, they often need only a focused set of features: navigating to declarations, finding references, code completion, and renames.
These capabilities are exactly what the Language Server Protocol was built for: implementing language support once, and reusing it in any LSP-capable editor. And it’s not only humans who benefit. Agents can call into an LSP directly, producing faster, more deterministic results – and, importantly, consuming fewer tokens.
These are the workflows we want to accommodate with our extension and the underlying IntelliJ IDEA’s Language Server and Debug Adapter.
Cursor collaboration
When we set out to bring IntelliJ IDEA’s language intelligence beyond our own IDE, Cursor was a natural first partner. 
Their team collaborated closely with us throughout the development of the extension, battle-testing it and making sure Java and Kotlin developers get a seamless experience inside Cursor from the moment they open a project. 
We’re glad to work with JetBrains to bring Java and Kotlin language intelligence to Cursor. With Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA, developers get IntelliJ IDEA’s code analysis, navigation, and refactoring while they work with Cursor’s agents.
— Rohan Shah, Product, SpaceX AI
What’s in 1.0
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA is powered by the same Java and Kotlin language technology as the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE. 1.0 brings a focused set of capabilities to VS Code and Cursor, including:
Java, Kotlin, and mixed-language project support
Smart code completion, navigation, and code analysis
Refactorings and editor assistance
Maven, Gradle, and Bazel build tool support
Fast, reliable performance even on large projects and monorepos
Support for test runners right now for JUnit
Powerful debugging capabilities, including emulated breakpoints and async stack traces




The full feature list is in our documentation.
For Cursor, there is dedicated support for the Agents Window. It may use its own instance of the Language Server to provide analysis capabilities based on IntelliJ IDEA’s inspections. This includes nullability support with JSpecify and for Spring Framework’s specifics.




Getting started
Install Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA from the Visual Studio Marketplace or the Open VSX registry.
Install from Visual Studio Marketplace
Install from Open VSX Registry
Once installed, open your Java or Kotlin project in VS Code or Cursor. The extension analyzes your project, imports it based on any Maven, Gradle, or Bazel build files it finds, and enables Java and Kotlin language features in the editor.
Compatibility notice
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA includes code analysis and quick-fixes that overlap with Red Hat’s and Oracle’s Java extensions. To avoid duplicated or conflicting behavior, we recommend disabling those extensions while using ours.
We have, however, made sure that our extension works well with others, like Spring Tools from the Spring Team.
Licensing
With version 1.0, the extension moves out of its free preview phase. Using it now requires an IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate subscription after a 30-day trial period during which you can try out its full feature set for free.
The same license covers IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin capabilities everywhere you work – the IntelliJ IDEA desktop IDE, VS Code-based editors like Cursor, and other supported environments. You can review pricing here.
Note: The license is explicitly designed for human use; we’ll release an update regarding licensing models for purely agentic use soon.
Coming next: Agentic and terminal-based workflows
Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA 1.0 in the editor is just one milestone. 
In one of the next releases, agents that you orchestrate in the Agents view in Cursor or VS Code will also be able to call the LSP directly when writing code, leading to faster, better, or cheaper results.
In parallel, we’ve been running experiments applying the same LSP- and DAP-backed intelligence to fully agentic, terminal-based workflows – think Claude Code or Codex calling directly into IntelliJ IDEA’s Java and Kotlin understanding. News on this will also be announced soon.
Feedback and support
We’re still listening – Java and Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA 1.0 is a milestone, not the finish line. Tell us what works, what doesn’t, and what you want next. Leave a comment here, open a ticket in our issue tracker, or submit a support request using this form.
Thank you to everyone who tested the preview, and to the Cursor team for launching this with us.

posts.title: How Netflix Made AI Coding Agents More Efficient with JetBrains IDE Intelligence
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Netflix plugged JetBrains’ headless code-intelligence engine – the same one behind IntelliJ IDEA – into Claude Code and Codex, then benchmarked it against a variety of scenarios. The details and numbers are available below.




At a glance

CompanyNetflix – Application Development Platform (ADP), GenAI Platform, and Agentic SDLC teams
ChallengeCoding agents were struggling to navigate Java/Kotlin code, especially across compiled library (JAR) boundaries
TechnologyJetBrains IDE code intelligence for Java, built on the same code-indexing engine that powers IntelliJ IDEA, run headlessly with no IDE open.
Netflix’s roleBuilt the daemon and CLI needed to make the LSP callable by an agent – infrastructure that JetBrains hadn’t shipped yet
ResultTypically 20–30% more efficient (fewer tokens, less time), and up to about 65% in the best case, on real programming tasks – the size of the gain depends on the model, the agent, and the task, generally larger for stronger models and higher effort settings
Evaluated onTwo real codebases – an internal production service and Netflix’s open-source DGS Framework – across several current coding agents and models, July–August 2026





The goal: Increase agent ROI
JetBrains and Netflix set out to give coding agents accurate, IntelliJ IDEA-grade code understanding in headless environments – with no IntelliJ IDEA instance running.
“Coding agents like Claude Code are slow and unreliable at navigating Java/Kotlin code, especially across library (JAR) boundaries. We integrated a headless JetBrains IDE’s code engine to give agents IntelliJ IDE-grade code intelligence in headless environments, with no IDE running. We created a benchmark with real programming tasks, which shows that with the JetBrains IDE’s code engine, agents are consistently more efficient – using fewer tokens and less time, with the exact gain depending on the model.”
— Paul Bakker, Staff Software Engineer, Netflix
The JAR problem Netflix is trying to solve that Paul describes above: JVM projects typically ship libraries as JAR files only, never as source. Agents have to unzip the JARs (guessing which ones matter), potentially decompile class files, then grep through that incomplete view.
The solution: JetBrains IDE intelligence
JetBrains has spent years building the code intelligence engine behind IntelliJ IDEA. It is based on a deterministic index of your project source files, including all libraries. This intelligence is now exposed via an LSP and available in VS Code-compatible editors. Netflix worked with a headless build of that engine.
The LSP alone isn’t enough for a coding agent to use directly: It’s just a server speaking a protocol, with no easy way for an agent to call it and no built-in process management to reuse a running instance between calls. Netflix closed that gap themselves using the daemon and CLI described in the next section.
Architecture in detail: Keeping the index warm
Building an index for a project takes real time, just as opening a large project in IntelliJ IDEA for the first time does. A coding agent calls the LSP in many small, fine-grained steps, and a realistic task needs several such calls. If each one spun up a fresh LSP server, every single call would incur a multi-second cold-start cost – even on a project whose index had already been built a minute earlier.
A daemon process is required to avoid the overhead of cold-starting the LSP server process on repeated calls. JetBrains is working on delivering a daemon, but no daemon was available by the time of evaluation, so Netflix has built one for their own needs:
Each tool call was short-lived and stateless – it just shelled out to the CLI.
The daemon is the part that stays up: Its session manager routes each call by project root to the matching server process, which holds that project’s index in memory.
A second call against the same project skips indexing entirely and goes straight to a warm server over stdio.
Both the daemon and CLI are developed in Java and distributed as a GraalVM executable, so there is no startup or runtime overhead from the JVM.
How Netflix measured the ROI of JetBrains IDE intelligence
To understand if (and to what extent) JetBrains IDE intelligence improves the performance of a coding agent, a benchmark suite was developed. Same model, same task, same codebase – the only variable was whether the agent could invoke the JetBrains IDE intelligence. Results are reported as the performance difference between runs with JetBrains IDE intelligence versus runs without it.
Evaluation environment and approach:

DatasetsTwo real codebases: An internal service (medium-size project) using Spring Boot 4 and Gradle.
Netflix’s own open-source DGS Framework – a public, mixed Kotlin/Java GraphQL framework.
TasksTwo task types:
Small/focused tasks where the agent attempts to understand specifics in the codebase, e.g. “where is this interface used in the project”, “what implementations exist of this interface”, “what is the structure of this class”.
Full end-to-end tasks, such as implementing a new feature, refactoring a class, or removing code.
ModelsClaude Code with Opus 5 (medium/high effort)
Claude Code with Sonnet 5 (medium/high effort)
Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol (medium/high effort)
ScoringWhile the most important metrics in the experiment were token consumption and time to completion, LLM as a judge was implemented for checking correctness. It works against a reference change set for end-to-end tasks and applies deterministic scoring metric for navigation tasks.
Outlier handlingA task that crashed, hit a budget cap, or thrashed in either arm was excluded from both, so one blow-up couldn’t skew the comparison.





The benchmarks were run multiple times to validate the results and see the effects of changes from new LSP releases.
Results
Across every model, agent, and task type tested, JetBrains IDE intelligence made coding agents more efficient overall – typically 20–30% more efficient, and up to about 65% in the best case, depending on the specific model, agent, and task. The stronger models, with higher effort, saw the largest gains. These models are more expensive, so efficiency improvements matter more, but these models are also better at using indexes effectively.
~25%
Average gain
20–30%
Typical range
~65%
Best case
Configuration
          Code navigation
          End-to-end
        
Strongest model, high effort
          ~65%
          ~24%
        
Mid model, high effort
          ~29%
          ~30%
        
Mid model, medium effort
          ~24%
          ~22%
        
Lighter configuration, high effort
          ~17%*
          ~21%
        
These numbers are a snapshot, not a fixed benchmark result. Every new model release changes how agents search, reason, and use tools, so the exact percentages will keep moving – which is why this write-up reports ranges rather than per-model results. What held up across Netflix’s runs is the general shape: every model and agent tested became more efficient, the largest gains came from the strongest model at a high-effort setting, and the size of the gain differed noticeably from one model to the next.
Code-navigation tasks: More efficient across the board, correctness held or improved
Every model and effort level tested used fewer tokens with JetBrains IDE intelligence – no exceptions there – with savings ranging from roughly 15% to 60%. The size of the gain depended mostly on the model: the strongest model saw by far the largest improvements, while lighter-weight configurations landed at the lower end of both ranges. Correctness held steady in most runs and improved in two – it never dropped.
For the code-navigation tasks specifically, one tool/model combination already batches multiple search calls into a single command, so both with and without JetBrains IDE intelligence, it only makes one tool call there. Calling into JetBrains IDE intelligence is a little slower for that one call than the batched search command – which is what produced the clear lack of time benefit for that combination, not a fair reflection of real-world use. That’s why the broader end-to-end task suite is the more reliable read on time instead, where JetBrains IDE intelligence was faster across every model and agent tested.
End-to-end tasks: Consistently more efficient, correctness unaffected
On the expanded end-to-end run, correctness held steady everywhere across every model and agent tested, so the benefit shows up entirely in efficiency, not in whether the task got done. Every model and agent combination was roughly 10–30% more efficient with JetBrains IDE intelligence, looking at time to completion and token spend. A lot of this is explained by requiring fewer tool calls to come to the same conclusions.
Other evaluated alternatives
Before committing to the described approach, Netflix ruled out two others. The first rejected was a homegrown internal CLI that connected to a running IntelliJ IDEA instance to get access to a project index. The process is similar to what this article describes, but it requires an IDE to be running. This approach didn’t fit headless agents for environments like Otto, Bitbot, distributed refactoring tooling, CI, etc.
Second, an existing Eclipse LSP, which is used for Java in VS Code, was considered. But for Netflix’s build system (Gradle-based), it just didn’t work.
What’s next
Where Netflix goes from here
After the test, Netflix concluded that “the benchmarks show that there is a benefit to having a deterministic intelligence layer alongside your agent”. Of course, it doesn’t cut every coding-agent task by a fixed percentage. But for this specific problem – resolving real structure across JAR boundaries – the benefit is large, holds across models, and doesn’t cost anything in correctness.
Netflix plans to run the same benchmark methodology against Python, TypeScript/JavaScript, and Go. Coding agents for those languages have similar problems. But of course, the ways libraries are downloaded in a project vary by language, so the mechanics of the issues and possible solutions differ. JetBrains plans to continue the collaboration and support this evaluation further.
JetBrains’ take: The LSP is just one step, not the destination
JetBrains IDE intelligence for Java has been tested by Netflix and is now shipped as part of the Java & Kotlin by IntelliJ IDEA extension. JetBrains also continues experiments with the LSP+CLI approach and will report the results once ready.
The LSP’s basic primitive is a position in a text document. The specification defines a position as “between two characters, like an insert cursor in an editor”. That’s a natural primitive for a human working at a keyboard. But agents don’t really think in terms of cursor locations. They ask questions about the program, like “Why is this call inside createUser() unresolved?” and “Which tests are covering this method?”, etc. It’s about understanding relationships between parts of the code rather than looking at cursor positions. And a text position is a fragile identity – inserting one character before any given position causes that position to move.
What an agent needs isn’t a sharper cursor, but a layer that provides answers formulated in the same way as the tasks themselves – i.e. in terms of symbols, diagnostics, test relations, runtime behavior – and returns enough context to reason about the answer, not just locations in a text document.
“That’s what I mean by a code engine: not another protocol that lets an agent imitate editor interaction, but a set of precise operations over program structure and execution – one that returns enough context to actually reason about the result. LSP is useful, but it shouldn’t define the final agent-facing abstraction. Build agent tooling as if the agent were a tiny human at an editor, and you force it to speak in cursor coordinates. Agents need a code engine, not a virtual editor.”
— Aleksey Stukalov, IDE Division Lead, JetBrains
The Netflix numbers prove code intelligence is worth paying for. Deciding what shape that intelligence takes is the challenge that lies ahead.

posts.title: MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate Available
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
MPS 2026.2 is almost ready! Today we’re making a release candidate build available so you can try out the upcoming release ahead of its official launch. Download MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate now:
DOWNLOAD MPS 2026.2 Release Candidate
Along with numerous bug fixes, the RC brings several key improvements to the previous 2026.2 EAP1 build.
Linux ARM64 support
MPS is now available for Linux on ARM64 (AArch64), with a matching bundled JetBrains Java Runtime.
You can also build standalone MPS-based applications (RCPs) for Linux ARM64. The Build Script Wizard now includes a Linux ARM64 distribution in its generated build scripts alongside the existing platform distributions.
TAR imports in Build Language
Build Language now supports importing archive contents directly into distribution layouts using the new import files from tar and files from tar entries.
You can import files from plain TAR archives or archives compressed with gzip or bzip2. The source can be an archive file or another TAR layout defined in the build script.
When importing into a TAR layout, symbolic links and file permissions are preserved. This is particularly useful when packaging platform-specific plugins and native libraries, as symbolic links remain links instead of becoming duplicate copies of their targets.
Archive packaging changes
MPS 2026.2 preserves symbolic links and file permissions when packaging platform-specific plugins. Previously, symbolic links were sometimes replaced with copies of their targets, causing large native libraries to be included more than once, particularly on macOS.
macOS archive distributions now use .tar.gz instead of .zip to preserve symbolic links. The Build Script Wizard generates the same archive format for standalone macOS applications.
Projectional Agent Toolkit enhancements
Projectional Agent Toolkit has received a major boost in performance and capabilities.
Performance
Your AI agents can now cut back on token usage on common tasks like DSL modeling or implementing language definitions. In our measurements using Claude Code + Opus 5 and 5.5, the savings exceeded 50%.
This improvement is the result of a substantial rework of the MPS MCP API:
Consistent parameter naming, null and default-value handling, and error reporting.
More precise descriptions in the skills and tool documentation.
Bulk operations where they provide the greatest benefit, with compact summaries instead of huge payloads.
Small read results included directly in responses, with large dumps written to files only when needed.
One-shot model validation to check full models without round-trip overhead.
Fast concept discovery using lightweight, structure-only metadata views instead of full AST dumps.
Fail-fast checks that reject invalid search scopes and mutation inputs instead of returning incomplete results.
Helper scripts included with the skills, so agents spend less time reinventing common MPS tasks.
Clearer project targeting when several MPS or IDE projects are open.
Typesystem MCP tool
The Typesystem MCP tool enables agents to:
Understand node types and typesystem messages.
Compare types and determine the expected type for a role.
Trace type calculations and debug typesystem rules.
Identify the typesystem rule responsible for a reported typesystem error.

Other newly added MCP tools
In addition to the Typesystem MCP tool, we’ve added several more MCP tools to cover other core aspects of MPS development. The new tools enable agents to:
Invoke intentions and quick-fixes.
Automatically keep their skill database up to date with the MPS instance they connect to.
Read and filter the content of MPS logs.
Open, close, and create MPS projects.
Automatically correct SModel expressions in parsed Java statements, helping agents author concept functions and behavior methods.

Import dialog reworked: Select models and languages to import
The Import dialog has undergone a major overhaul to fix functional issues and bring its appearance in line with the rest of the platform.
When pasting code between models, only the models and languages you actually select in the dialog are imported. Previously, the dialog ignored your selection.
If the dialog offers only one suggestion, you can now deselect it. Previously, the single suggestion could not be deselected.
Both the model and language lists now have checkboxes for individual entries and a header checkbox to select or deselect all entries. The header checkbox shows an indeterminate state when only some entries are selected.
Diff dialog and tab improvements
We’ve made quite a few minor changes to bring the Diff dialog’s look and feel in line with the rest of the platform.
The model viewer now has its own icon instead of sharing the side-by-side icon. The top bar is vertically centered, and the left and right panels match the splitter background.
Diffs of added or deleted models and of per-root persistence models now have aligned title bars, so separator lines no longer drift when one side is empty.
Change markers on the scrollbar now remain in the right position when the dialog or editor is resized. Previously, a marker would sometimes jump to an unrelated location. The fix was made in the shared editor gutter, so regular editor error and warning markers are covered, too.
Editor hints defined in your language now appear on the left (read-only) diff panel for file-per-root persistence and on the right panel for per-root persistence models.
You can review the complete list of fixed issues here.
Your JetBrains MPS team

posts.title: What Makes a Great KotlinConf Proposal?
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is now open! We invite developers from across the Kotlin community to bring their ideas, experiences, and expertise to the stage in Kraków.
Do you have a Kotlin lesson or discovery that could help other developers? Perhaps you solved a difficult technical problem, introduced Kotlin into an existing codebase, built something unexpected, or learned valuable lessons from an approach that did not go according to plan.
That experience could become a KotlinConf talk.
Submit your proposal
However, turning an idea into a convincing conference proposal can be challenging, especially if you’ve never submitted one before. How do you know whether your experience is worth sharing? What do reviewers notice first? How detailed should your abstract be? And how can you make a familiar topic stand out?
To help you prepare your submission, we asked Kotlin developers, developer advocates, experienced speakers, and KotlinConf program committee members what makes a strong proposal. Alongside practical advice for shaping your title, abstract, and takeaways, we have added a new section answering an especially important question: What do reviewers notice first when they open a proposal?
First-time speaker? Submit your idea anyway!
It’s easy to assume that a KotlinConf talk must begin with a groundbreaking discovery, a major production system, or years of speaking experience. In reality, a valuable talk can begin with a simple idea or a lesson learned while solving an everyday development problem.
You don’t need to know everything about Kotlin – you need something useful to share and a clear idea of who it could help.
Pamela Hill-Galloway. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
Submit your idea anyway! There have been some wildly successful talks at KotlinConf that started out as just a simple idea.
If you’re unsure whether your topic would interest anyone, discuss it with the people around you. Explain the idea to colleagues, friends, members of a user group, or people in the Kotlin community. Their questions and reactions can help you understand which parts are most valuable.
Marcin Mycek. Product Manager, Kotlin Build Tools
LinkedIn
If you can find one interested person, there are probably more! If you can find at least two people around you who find the topic interesting and can listen for more than five minutes, it is already a decent candidate.
Previous conference experience is not required. A clear, authentic proposal based on something you understand and care about can be more compelling than a polished proposal with little substance behind it.
Start with the story you want to tell
Before writing the title or opening the submission form, identify the central story behind your talk.
“A talk about coroutines” or “a session about Kotlin Multiplatform” describes a subject, but it doesn’t explain what makes the session valuable.
Ask yourself:
What problem, question, or opportunity did you encounter?
Why was it important or difficult?
What did you try?
What surprised you?
What succeeded and what did not?
What did you learn that other developers could apply?
Your story doesn’t need to come from a large company or a system used by millions of people. A focused lesson from a small project can be just as useful if it offers an original insight or explains a difficult subject clearly.
Try summarizing the idea in one sentence, for example:
This talk will show [audience] how we [solved or explored something], what we learned, and how they can apply those lessons.
If you can’t complete that sentence clearly, the idea may need a little more development before you start writing the proposal.
What do reviewers notice first?
The title may be the first line reviewers read, but the overall level of care quickly becomes visible.
Reviewers consider not only whether the topic is interesting, but also whether the speaker can explain it clearly. A thoughtful title, focused description, concrete takeaways, and careful formatting show that you have spent time developing your idea.
Pamela Hill-Galloway. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
I can sum it up by saying that the care you take in writing the proposal is probably more obvious than people think. If I can see that you took the time to come up with a catchy or descriptive title that works well with the content, I am more comfortable giving you a thumbs-up to speak at KotlinConf. If your description is so short or so long, or so clearly AI-generated, that you cannot express your idea clearly and neatly, I will probably not vote positively for your talk.
This doesn’t mean you need to use complicated language or create a perfect marketing pitch. It means giving reviewers enough information to understand your idea and showing that the proposal represents your own experience and voice.
Marcin Moskała’s Taming Asynchronous Beasts: Debugging and Performance Tuning in a Coroutine World provides a good example of a precise promise: “You’ll learn how to effectively use built-in tools, recognize problematic patterns, and implement proven optimization strategies.”
Write a clear and informative title
A strong title should give reviewers, and eventually attendees, an accurate idea of what the talk will cover.
Creativity can make a title memorable, but clarity should come first. Avoid titles that rely entirely on a joke, reference, or metaphor without explaining the subject.
Pamela Hill-Galloway. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
A carefully-selected title can make all the difference! Audience members often lack the time or attention span to read more than the title when deciding whether to attend a talk. Prefer clarity over a catchy or fun title that doesn’t give a good idea of what the talk is about in a nutshell.
Compare the following title examples:
Too broad:
Our Multiplatform Journey
More informative:
What We Learned Migrating Our Mobile App to Kotlin Multiplatform
Too vague:
Coroutines Gone Wild
More informative:
Debugging Coroutine Performance Problems in Production
Too general:
Building Better APIs
More informative:
Designing Type-Safe Kotlin APIs That Are Difficult to Misuse
A good title usually communicates at least two of the following:
The main topic
The problem or question
The context in which it was explored
The practical benefit for attendees
The expected experience level
You can still use humor or wordplay, but make sure the title does not hide what the session is actually about.
Build your abstract around a clear journey
Your abstract doesn’t need to contain your entire presentation. However, it should provide enough detail for reviewers to understand the problem, the direction of the talk, and its value.
Two or three focused paragraphs will usually communicate more than either a single vague sentence or a very long description covering every detail.
Sebastian Sellmair. Software Developer and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, YouTube 
Talking at KotlinConf is a great experience and a huge achievement for any Kotlin developer. While choosing a great title, having highly polished animations, and curating high-quality memes might enhance your talk, the most important thing is having a story worth telling. Do you have something novel and technically interesting to present? Can you break down a topic in a way that is engaging and truly fun? Can you inspire fellow developers?
 
Márton Braun. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn 
While we don’t need a full script for your talk as the abstract, we’re also unlikely to accept a talk where the abstract is just a single sentence. Two or three paragraphs are usually enough to provide meaningful detail.
A simple structure can help:
The context
Introduce the situation and the audience likely to recognize it.
The challenge
Explain the problem, limitation, or question that motivated the work.
Jodie Burchell. Developer Advocate and Data Scientist
LinkedIn, Mastodon, BlueSky
Hook your audience by telling them the problem you’re going to be solving. People love mystery books for a reason, and that’s because they build up a bit of suspense before they jump into the solution. A great proposal will do the same thing.
 
The approach
Describe what you explored, implemented, compared, or discovered.
The outcome
Clarify what attendees will learn and how they can use it.
A strong takeaway can be as concrete as the one from Tadeas Kriz’s Dependencies and Kotlin/Native: “Learn how native dependencies interact, how they are loaded, and the unexpected complexities of the native world.”
Chantal Loncle. Software Developer, Exposed, JetBrains 
LinkedIn
Avoid vague promises. Instead, use action verbs and specific outcomes to describe the exact capabilities and transformations the audience will gain. Will they leave your talk feeling that their time was well spent? If so, what practical knowledge, immediately applicable skills, or high-value tools will they take with them?
For example:
Maintaining separate Android and iOS implementations allowed our teams to move independently, but it also resulted in duplicated business logic and inconsistent behavior between the applications.
In this session, we’ll examine how we introduced Kotlin Multiplatform gradually, beginning with one shared feature rather than attempting a complete migration. We’ll discuss how we selected the first component, structured the shared code, tested it across platforms, and worked with the existing native applications.
You’ll leave with a practical framework for evaluating where to introduce shared code, which challenges to expect, and how to plan an incremental Kotlin Multiplatform adoption without rebuilding your entire application.
The example establishes the problem, explains what the session will cover, and gives the audience a reason to attend. It doesn’t reveal every detail, but it makes a concrete promise.
Think like an attendee
A strong proposal doesn’t focus only on what the speaker wants to present. It also explains what the audience will gain.
Ask yourself:
Who is this session for?
What knowledge should attendees already have?
What problem will the talk help them solve?
What will they understand or be able to do afterward?
Why should they choose this session over another talk happening at the same time?
Svetlana Isakova. Team Lead in Kotlin Developer Advocacy, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X
When submitting a talk, think like an attendee. Would you want to sit through this? What’s in it for the audience? That’s why we ask about key takeaways. What do you want people to learn, try, do, or feel inspired by?
 
Avoid broad promises such as:
“You will learn best practices.”
“We will explore Kotlin Multiplatform.”
“This talk will cover coroutines.”
Instead, describe specific outcomes:
Attendees will learn how to identify and debug three common coroutine performance problems.
Attendees will understand how we structured shared code across Android and iOS.
Attendees will be able to evaluate whether the approach fits their own project.
Attendees will learn which parts of our migration worked, which did not, and what we would change today.
Specific takeaways make the proposal easier to evaluate. If the talk is selected, they also help attendees decide whether it is relevant to them.
Make a familiar topic feel fresh
Your subject doesn’t have to be completely new. Many valuable conference talks revisit established technologies from perspectives that have not been explored in the same way before.
If you are proposing a popular topic, identify what makes your version distinctive. This could be:
A real production case
An unusual scale or environment
A surprising result
A failed approach and what it taught you
A comparison between several possible solutions
A gradual migration rather than a greenfield implementation
An unconventional use of Kotlin
A personal experience that challenges a common assumption
A particularly clear way of explaining a difficult concept
For example, “Introduction to Kotlin Multiplatform” is broad and familiar. “What Broke When We Introduced Kotlin Multiplatform Into a Seven-Year-Old Mobile App” offers a specific context and creates curiosity.
Be honest about trade-offs. A talk doesn’t need to present a flawless success story. Explaining what failed, what changed, and what you would do differently can be especially useful to other developers.
Chantal Loncle. Software Developer, Exposed, JetBrains 
LinkedIn
Bringing a real, practical narrative to a familiar topic can strengthen a proposal. Be honest about what broke, what made your team unhappy, or what you would do differently if you could turn back the clock. A familiar issue can feel fresh when you look at it from the perspective of someone who will encounter the same problem for the first time tomorrow.
Rather than providing another general overview, build the talk around one specific pain point or discovery and introduce broader themes only where they support that story. A takeaway that attendees can immediately apply to their work can also help distinguish the proposal from a basic tutorial.
Keep the proposal relevant to KotlinConf
KotlinConf welcomes talks about backend development, Android, multiplatform development, web, desktop, AI, language design, tooling, libraries, developer experience, and other parts of the Kotlin ecosystem.
Whatever your area, the role Kotlin plays in the story should be clear.
Márton Braun. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
Keep in mind that your talk should be related to Kotlin! For example, not every Android talk is necessarily a good fit for the KotlinConf audience. Or talks about Jetpack Compose often cover things that work the exact same way with Compose Multiplatform, and the latter is much more likely to be accepted at KotlinConf!
An Android topic, for example, is not automatically a KotlinConf topic. The proposal becomes more relevant when it explains how Kotlin influenced the solution, explores a Kotlin-specific technical decision, or provides lessons that Kotlin developers can apply.
Ask yourself:
Why is this a Kotlin story?
Which parts of the experience are especially relevant to Kotlin developers?
Would the proposal still be essentially the same if Kotlin were removed from it?
If the answer to the final question is yes, strengthen the connection to Kotlin before submitting.
Anshika Koul’s Kotlin Multiplatform’s Cross-Platform Brilliance at Norway’s 377-Year-Old National Postal Service offers a clear example of a Kotlin-centered takeaway: “We’ll learn how KMP provides a unified framework for code sharing and execution across various platforms to solve the challenge of different codebases targeting different runtimes.”
Sound confident, but stay true to yourself
Your proposal should show that you understand what you want to share and why it matters.
This doesn’t mean exaggerating your expertise or pretending that you have no doubts. It means presenting the idea as a clear statement rather than repeatedly questioning its value.
Marcin Mycek. Product Manager, Kotlin Build Tools
LinkedIn
Keep statements as statements and questions as questions. It is normal to doubt yourself; everybody does, but a common mistake is to let it show in the text, for example, by changing statements into questions. Read your submission, or even better, ask someone else to read it, and ask yourself: Does this person sound convinced about what they want to tell?
For example:
Uncertain:
Could Kotlin Multiplatform possibly help teams reduce duplicated business logic? In this talk, we might find out.
More confident:
In this talk, I’ll show how our team used Kotlin Multiplatform to reduce duplicated business logic, including where sharing code helped and where it did not.
Confidence should not erase your personality. The proposal should still sound like you.
Marcin Mycek. Product Manager, Kotlin Build Tools
LinkedIn
Stay true to yourself! It is important to make sure that your submission can be understood by others. A great practice is to give it to a few people you trust and ask what they understood from it and how it made them feel. However, keep your soul in it. A lot of great talks are quirky, do not follow every best practice, and people are there for it.
Advice and templates can help you organize your thoughts, but they shouldn’t make every proposal sound identical. Your perspective, language, humor, and enthusiasm are part of what makes the submission memorable.
Show reviewers how you communicate
Examples of previous talks help reviewers understand your presentation style and energy. If you have recordings from conferences, meetups, webinars, or livestreams, include the most relevant ones.
If you’re a first-time speaker and don’t have a formal recording, you can record yourself explaining part of the proposed talk. A simple laptop recording is enough. It doesn’t need professional lighting, editing, or production.
Svetlana Isakova. Team Lead in Kotlin Developer Advocacy, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X
Examples of your talks help us make better choices. If you’re a first-time speaker and don’t have recordings, no worries! You can simply record yourself (even just part of your proposed talk) on your laptop and share the link. We would really appreciate it.
Depending on the topic, you can also include:
A technical article
An open-source project
Documentation you have written
A short technical demonstration
A podcast or meetup appearance
Other work connected to the proposed session
These materials support your proposal, but they don’t replace a clear title, abstract, and set of takeaways. Reviewers should still be able to understand the session from the submission itself.
Choose the format that fits the idea
Not every subject needs a full-length session.
A focused lesson, experiment, side project, or surprising discovery may work better as a lightning talk. A subject that involves significant technical context, several connected lessons, or a detailed demonstration may require a regular session.
Choose the format according to the amount of meaningful material you have. If you need to repeat yourself or add unnecessary content to fill a regular session, consider proposing a lightning talk instead.
Márton Braun. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
Don’t forget that we also accept lightning talks! If you feel like your content would have to be padded to fill a regular session, it might be more enjoyable as a lightning talk.
You can also submit more than one proposal if you have several distinct ideas. Each submission should have its own story, audience, and takeaways rather than being a minor variation of another proposal.
Pamela Hill-Galloway. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
Submit more than one talk! It gives you more chances to join in on the KotlinConf fun.
Review the proposal before submitting
Once you have completed your draft, step away from it and return later from the perspective of someone encountering the idea for the first time.
Check whether your proposal answers the following questions:
Can someone understand the subject from the title?
Is the connection to Kotlin clear?
Does the abstract identify a real problem, question, or story?
Is it clear who the session is for?
Are the takeaways concrete?
Does the proposal explain what makes your perspective different?
Is the scope realistic for the selected format?
Does the writing sound confident and authentic?
Have you checked the spelling, grammar, links, and formatting?
Does the proposal sound like the person who will deliver the talk?
Ask someone else to review it, too. Rather than simply asking whether they like it, ask them to describe what they think the talk will cover and what they expect to learn. Their answer will show whether the proposal communicates what you intended.
Chantal Loncle. Software Developer, Exposed, JetBrains
LinkedIn
Double-check that the intended audience level aligns with the description and expected takeaways. Review the proposal from the perspective of someone you hope will be in the audience. Does it make sense as it is, or is it missing context that may be obvious to you but not to the reviewer or the future audience they are keeping in mind?
AI tools may help you check grammar or organize your thoughts, but the final proposal should reflect your own experience, ideas, and voice. A polished abstract without specific or authentic insight won’t be as convincing as one that clearly represents the speaker behind it.
Márton Braun. Developer Advocate, KotlinConf Program Committee member, and KotlinConf speaker
X, BlueSky, LinkedIn
Your submission should show that you’ve put some thought and energy into preparing it. Check your submission for formatting issues and typos, and please don’t submit abstracts that were generated by LLMs.
Your Kotlin story could take the stage
You don’t need to know everything about Kotlin or have years of conference experience to submit a proposal. You need a useful story, an understanding of who it can help, and a clear explanation of why it matters.
Not every strong proposal can be selected. Conference programs must balance subjects, formats, experience levels, and audience interests. If your submission is not accepted, continue refining the idea, sharing your knowledge, and looking for other opportunities to present it.
Your experience might be exactly what another Kotlin developer needs to hear.
The KotlinConf 2027 Call for Papers is open! Share your experience, ideas, and Kotlin expertise with the community in Kraków.
Submit your proposal

posts.title: Boost Your Pipeline: Top 6 CI/CD Integrations for Qodana
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Your CI/CD pipeline builds fast, but does it build right? While your automated builds and deployments handle the mechanics of software delivery, catching code quality issues often falls to manual reviews, which, while hugely valuable, can sometimes miss more subtle problems.
That’s where Qodana changes the game by bringing the power of IntelliJ IDEA’s inspection engine directly into your workflow with CI/CD integrations.
Qodana seamlessly integrates with several major CI/CD platforms, extending the same intelligent code analysis you rely on in your IDE to every commit and pull request. You can automate quality gates that prevent problematic code from reaching production, no matter which platform your team prefers.
This compatibility means you can maintain coding standards without disrupting existing workflows or learning new tools.
Table of Contents

Why integrate static code analysis with CI/CD pipelines?
1. GitHub Actions
Integrating Qodana with GitHub Actions

2. GitLab
Integrating Qodana with GitLab

3. TeamCity
Integrating Qodana with TeamCity

4. Jenkins
Integrating Qodana with Jenkins

5. Azure Pipelines
Integrating Qodana with Azure Pipelines

6. CircleCI
Integrating Qodana with CircleCI

Make code quality part of your workflow with CI/CD static code analysis

Why integrate static code analysis with CI/CD pipelines?
Integrating CI/CD static code analysis transforms how your team approaches code quality. Instead of discovering issues after deployment (when they’re expensive to fix), you can spot problems immediately as part of your existing development workflow. This is the essence of a ‘shift-left’ approach, where you’re moving quality checks to earlier in the lifecycle, so developers get faster feedback and teams spend less time reworking code.
Automated quality enforcement ensures every team member follows the same coding standards, no matter their experience level or tool preferences. When Qodana runs on every commit, you get consistent feedback that helps maintain code quality across your entire codebase.
Your CI/CD pipeline becomes more than just a deployment tool. It acts as a quality guardian,  blocking problematic code before it can impact your users.
But what are the top CI/CD integrations for Qodana? We’ll take a look at a few of the best and discuss how and why you should integrate them into your workflows.
1. GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions provides cloud-based CI/CD automation that integrates directly with your GitHub repositories. It supports all major programming languages and operating systems, with an extensive marketplace of pre-built GitHub Actions. 
This platform also excels at pull request workflows and offers flexible runner options for both public and private repositories.
Integrating Qodana with GitHub Actions
Qodana integrates with GitHub Actions through the official marketplace Action, making setup straightforward with a simple workflow file. The current v2025.2 Action provides comprehensive analysis capabilities and integrates seamlessly with GitHub’s pull request system. 
You’ll need to configure your QODANA_TOKEN as a repository secret and create a workflow file in your .github/workflows directory. For detailed configuration options and advanced setups, check the GitHub Actions documentation.

ProsCons
Reusable workflows and tight pull request integration make code reviews efficient.YAML configuration becomes complex for advanced setups and custom quality gates.
Quick-fix automation can create automatic pull requests with suggested code improvements.Runner costs for private repositories can escalate with heavy usage patterns.





2. GitLab
GitLab offers a complete DevOps platform with integrated CI/CD capabilities, available in both cloud and on-premises deployments. It supports over 60 programming languages and provides comprehensive project management features alongside its CI/CD functionality. GitLab’s strength lies in its all-in-one approach to software development workflows.
Integrating Qodana with GitLab
GitLab integration has been revolutionized with the new native GitLab CI/CD component introduced in 2025.1, replacing the previous Docker-only approach. This native component integration eliminates complexity while providing enhanced functionality. The component integrates directly with GitLab’s merge request UI, showing code quality reports alongside your existing code review process.

ProsCons
The native CI/CD component eliminates Docker complexity and streamlines setup significantly.Community users may experience slower queues during periods of high platform demand.
Results feed directly into your merge request UI with comprehensive code quality reports.Component features require GitLab 16.0 or higher for full functionality access.





For more information about GitLab CI/CD capabilities, check out the GitLab CI documentation.
3. TeamCity
TeamCity is JetBrains’ enterprise-focused CI server, offering both on-premises and cloud deployment options. It provides cross-platform support with advanced build management capabilities designed for scalability. As a JetBrains product, it offers deep integration opportunities with other JetBrains tools and development workflows.
Integrating Qodana with TeamCity
TeamCity offers the most streamlined Qodana integration through its native build runner, removing the need for Docker containers or complex YAML configurations. This native integration provides a GUI-based setup and built-in reporting capabilities. Your analysis results appear directly in TeamCity’s interface with comprehensive visualization and historical tracking. Find out more about how to integrate Qodana into TeamCity here. 






ProsCons
Native build runner with GUI configuration eliminates YAML complexity entirely.Windows build agents are currently not supported for Qodana analysis workflows.
Built-in reporting in TeamCity UI provides visual analysis results and trend tracking.Scaling your setup requires additional TeamCity agent licenses for larger teams.






Learn more about TeamCity capabilities, and read our detailed guide on integrating Qodana into TeamCity for step-by-step instructions.
4. Jenkins
Jenkins is the leading open-source automation server and features an extensive plugin ecosystem and self-hosted deployment model. It supports all major platforms and offers maximum customization flexibility through its pipeline scripting capabilities. Jenkins excels in complex enterprise environments where custom workflows are essential.
Check out the documentation.
Integrating Qodana with Jenkins
The Jenkins integration relies on Docker-based deployment through Jenkinsfile configuration, providing flexibility for complex pipeline requirements. It supports quality gates, baseline comparisons, and custom reporting workflows. You’ll configure Qodana as a Docker agent within your pipeline, allowing for sophisticated build orchestration.

ProsCons
Maximum customization through flexible pipeline scripting and an extensive plugin ecosystem.Requires Docker expertise for proper setup, maintenance, and troubleshooting.
An extensive plugin ecosystem enables custom quality gate workflows tailored to your needs.More complex configuration compared to native platform solutions available elsewhere.





For comprehensive Jenkins guidance, consult the Jenkins documentation.
5. Azure Pipelines
Azure Pipelines is Microsoft’s cloud CI/CD service offering Windows, Linux, and macOS support within the broader Azure DevOps ecosystem. It provides enterprise-grade features with strong integration across Microsoft’s development and cloud services. The platform excels in organizations already invested in Microsoft technologies. It was also one of the first pipelines Qodana could integrate into – this integration was introduced as early as 2022.
Integrating Qodana with Azure Pipelines
Azure Pipelines uses the QodanaScan@2025 task, enhanced with 2025.1 features that significantly improve the developer experience. The Azure Pipelines integration now displays results in the Extensions tab rather than cluttering build logs. This provides cleaner reporting and better visibility into code quality metrics.

ProsCons
Results appear in the Extensions tab instead of cluttering build logs, improving readability.Steeper learning curve for development teams not familiar with Microsoft tooling.

Seamless integration for teams already using Microsoft’s development ecosystem.Pipeline costs can escalate significantly with increased agent usage across large projects.





Find the Qodana extension in the Visual Studio Marketplace.
6. CircleCI




CircleCI is a cloud-native CI/CD platform with container-focused architecture and a credit-based pricing model. It excels at Docker workflows and provides predictable performance through its container-optimized infrastructure. The platform is particularly advantageous for teams prioritizing containerized development practices.
Integrating Qodana with CircleCI
The CircleCI integration provides container-optimized execution with excellent performance characteristics. Configuration involves declaring the orb in your .circleci/config.yml file.

ProsCons
Container-optimized execution delivers excellent performance for analysis workflows.Credit-based pricing can become expensive for large teams with frequent builds.
Established orb with regular updates and reliable maintenance since 2022.Less flexibility compared to self-hosted alternatives for custom enterprise requirements.





Explore the CircleCI Qodana orb at the CircleCI developer portal.
Make code quality part of your workflow with CI/CD static code analysis
These CI/CD integrations ensure consistent, automated code quality checks become part of your development process rather than an afterthought. By choosing the integration that fits your existing workflow, your team can enforce coding standards without disrupting productivity or requiring extensive retraining.
Qodana brings the same intelligent analysis that powers IntelliJ IDEA directly into your pipeline, no matter which platform your team prefers. Start with your preferred CI/CD tool today and make code quality an automated part of every commit your team makes.
Start a free trial and find out how Qodana can help you improve your codebase.

posts.title: How Cloud-Based Agent Sandboxing Works in Air
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Recently, we released a preview of cloud agents in JetBrains Air. Cloud agents let you run AI agents remotely in a JetBrains-managed cloud environment, giving them an isolated place to work without relying on your local machine.
Here’s what that looks like in practice. In this video, I start a task in IntelliJ IDEA, follow it from the browser and my phone, and review the agent’s changes when it’s done.






Cloud agents are currently available to organizational users via Air in IDEs and Air Teams in the browser, with a broader release for individual users planned later. But they are also part of a bigger question: how to run AI agents safely when they can read files, execute code, use tools, and interact with external services.
In this article, I’ll explain what agent sandboxing means, why it matters, what execution options exist today, and how cloud-based execution fits into the broader sandboxing picture.
Why AI agents need sandboxing
Sandboxing an AI agent is the practice of running the agent inside an isolated and tightly controlled environment that restricts what resources it can access and what actions it is allowed to perform. Rather than granting unrestricted access to the host system, network, or sensitive data, a sandbox enforces predefined boundaries around files, APIs, and external services, while applying least-privilege permissions, resource limits, audit mechanisms, and tracing.
This approach is important because modern AI agents can execute code, use tools, and act autonomously, which introduces risks such as unintended system modifications, data leakage, and exploitation if the agent behaves unexpectedly or is compromised. By containing the agent within well-defined security boundaries, sandboxing limits the impact of failures or attacks and provides a safer and more reliable foundation for deploying AI agents in development, enterprise, and production environments.
Five ways to run AI agents — and their security trade-offs
We can identify five main scenarios for launching agents, which can be grouped into two broad categories: local and remote.
Five ways to run an agent
Local setups share your machine. Remote setups move the agent somewhere else and isolate it by default.
Your machine
A working copy
Created fresh for each task
The agent

Mode
Isolated from your machine by default
Who sets it up


Local




Local workspaceWorks in your own working copy
Isolated by defaultNo – it can leave the working directory
Who sets it upNothing to set up; the client must enforce any limits





Git worktreeWorks in a separate copy on your machine
Isolated by defaultPartly – its file changes stay apart from yours, but it can still leave the directory
Who sets it upThe client creates the worktree


Remote






SSHWorks on a machine you provide, over SSH
Isolated by defaultYes
Who sets it upYou, manually






DockerWorks in a new container for each task,  locally or on a remote host. Docker Sandboxes use a microVM per agent.
Isolated by defaultYes
Who sets it upThe client, or org admins through Docker Sandboxes







CloudWorks in a new VM, microVM, or container for each task. Air uses a container inside a VM.
Isolated by defaultYes
Who sets it upAutomatic, from settings your team or org admin defines
By default, in local scenarios an agent can easily escape its current working directory either unintentionally or due to prompt injections. Their file system and network access can be limited via OS-level sandboxing tools (landrun on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS, and Sandboxie on Windows). However, it is then up to the client (the program that the user uses to interact with an agent or CLI tool like Claude Code or Codex) to wrap the launched agent and enforce required policies.
Remote execution provides better guarantees by default: The agent’s environment is isolated from the developer’s. The agent’s access to resources can be restricted via filesystem and network controls, limiting the area of impact. 
The main difference between the approaches lies primarily in the amount of manual configuration required. The SSH host requires a machine provided by the user and needs to be configured manually. Docker can be configured either by the client or by organization admins. Docker Sandboxes go a step further and run each agent in its own microVM. Cloud solutions should handle the configuration of the environments automatically based on the settings your team or organization admin defines.
How cloud agent sandboxing works in Air
The agentic core that powers cloud agents in Air follows the approach used by Docker Sandboxes. Each task starts a VM in the cloud (microVMs are coming soon), and the agent runs in a Docker container within that VM. The VM is considered untrusted: It is not reused between tasks and is allowed to access only limited internal resources. A proxy is set up in the VM, so all connections from the agent container are routed through it. 
Each Air task runs in its own VM, with the agent in a container behind a network proxy.



By default, the proxy allows connections only to a preset list of trusted source control and package registry domains, such as npm. You can add domains for your toolchains, package managers, or internal services, allow all domains, or turn internet access off completely.
Secrets are stored encrypted and exposed to the task as environment variables. Teammates can use a shared secret without seeing its value, and personal secrets stay private. Each task also acts within the developer’s own repository permissions, so it never sees a repository the developer can’t already access.
Where an agent runs matters as much as what it can do
Agent sandboxing is becoming an important part of working with AI agents safely. As agents become more capable and autonomous, the question is no longer only what they can do, but also where they run, what they can access, and how much impact they can have if something goes wrong.
Cloud-based execution is one way to provide stronger isolation by default, reduce local setup requirements, and give organizations more control over network access, environment configuration, and task execution policies.
Developers working in organizations can already try cloud agents in Air in JetBrains IDEs and Air Teams in the browser.
Have a question or feedback? Tag us on X at @getsome_air – Dennis and the Air team read mentions and reply.

posts.title: Lauterbach and JetBrains Announce TRACE32 Integration in CLion IDE
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Hoehenkirchen, Germany/Amsterdam, Netherlands — October 14, 2026 — Lauterbach and JetBrains have integrated TRACE32® debugging tools with CLion, JetBrains’ professional C and C++ tool. The integration enables embedded developers to debug applications on target hardware directly from CLion, bringing code editing, navigation, and hardware debugging into one development workflow.
Using the Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP), the integration connects CLion to TRACE32® through the TRACE32 Debug Adapter. Developers can control execution, step through code, and inspect variables in CLion while TRACE32® handles communication with the target hardware.
Two workflows are supported. Developers can launch a new TRACE32® PowerView session from CLion, using scripts to configure the connection and initialize the target, or attach to an existing TRACE32® instance. The integration requires CLion 2026.2.4 or later, TRACE32® PowerView 09.2026 (or build 195402), and TRACE32 Debug Adapter version 0.1.2 or later. Detailed configuration examples are documented in the Lauterbach knowledge base.
Lauterbach’s broader TRACE32® portfolio supports embedded development throughout the product life cycle, from pre-silicon development and prototyping to testing and in-field analysis. The tools combine PowerView debugging and tracing software with PowerDebug and PowerTrace hardware modules, helping engineers investigate system behavior, analyze performance, and measure code coverage across a wide range of processors and embedded targets.
CLion is the professional development environment where your C/C++ and embedded teams can run their agents, verify every change before it ships, and deliver to any target – desktop, server, or embedded hardware. It helps developers understand and maintain complex codebases, with support for embedded development workflows. The TRACE32® integration extends these workflows to debugging on target hardware from within the IDE.
“CLion helps developers write, refactor, debug, and test C and C++ code with smart navigation and cross-platform toolchains,” says Dr. Markus Herdin, Director of Marketing at Lauterbach GmbH. “With this TRACE32® integration, developers can use our debugging tools to investigate application behavior on target hardware directly from CLion.”
“For embedded developers, understanding the code is only part of the job. They also need to understand how it behaves on the target hardware,” says Artemy Pestretsov, Head of C/C++ Ecosystem at JetBrains. “Connecting TRACE32 with CLion brings those activities into the same workflow, helping developers investigate problems and verify changes in the environment where they write their code.”
Join a free webinar hosted by JetBrains and Lauterbach 
on October 27, 2026, at 2:00 pm (CET) / 1:00 pm (UTC) 
to see the integration in action.

posts.title: What We Heard at AGNTCon Europe
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
The night before AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe, we hosted the Agentic AI Foundation community at the JetBrains office in Amsterdam. The event filled up fast and went to a waitlist, which is not what I expected for a Wednesday evening discussion about how open foundations work.




Ibrahim Malik opening the evening.
The panel asked what happens when companies, maintainers, and contributors want different things from the same project. In other words, who gets to decide? That’s the oldest question in open source, and agents haven’t made it any easier. Nick Veenhof from GitLab, Alessandro Vozza from VOLT Datacenters, Miguel Luna from JetBrains, and I each came at it differently. My favorite line of the night was Nick’s. Talking about the infrastructure the Drupal Association runs so anyone can download project code, he said: “Someone needs to pay for the roads”. Paying keeps a project alive. Two days at the conference convinced me it doesn’t determine who decides. That goes to whoever has earned the trust, and you can’t buy trust. You earn it by doing the work, consistently and in the open.




Left to right: Nick Veenhof (GitLab), Miguel Luna and Katherine Druckman (JetBrains), Alessandro Vozza (VOLT Datacenters), and Bauke Brenninkmeijer (Orq.ai).
Review is the bottleneck now
I spent part of the summer on program committees for several events, reading talk proposals. A lot of them were AI-generated, polished, and interchangeable. Maintainers in working groups across open source describe the same thing – long AI-generated proposals that relitigate decisions already made. Their work shifts from building to explaining what was settled six months ago. Mine shifted from just choosing talks to working out which ones had enough real human experience behind them.
Dexter Horthy of HumanLayer came at the same problem from the other direction in his keynote, State of the Software Factory. He argued that code from unattended agents gets worse over time, so for now, people need to plan before they build and keep reading the code. His diagram added agentic code review and regression testing to the production pipeline, and he pointed out that review can still be the bottleneck. None of that is new, but his emphasis was the message. The hard part now is everything that comes after the code gets written. Someone has to understand what an agent produced and answer for it. Out on the show floor, one startup had built its entire booth around bugs written by agents.




Dexter Horthy’s “Lights-Off Software Factory”, the setup without human review that he argued against, from his keynote, State of the Software Factory.
What went wrong
A talk I keep thinking about was Nick Veenhof’s. He walked through a system he built for himself, 13 specialist agents, and one orchestrator, and he was honest about what failed. Tests passed while the wiring underneath was broken. A background job stopped for 46 days with no alert. An agent produced 80 fabricated data points that looked exactly like what he had asked for, and it took him two hours to catch them. His point was that complete and wrong is worse than partial and honest. He has been writing the whole thing up publicly, failures included.




A slide from Nick Veenhof’s talk, From Personal Agent To Org Catalog.
A good reason to show up
The conventions for how agents connect to tools, get traced, and stay secure are being written right now, in working groups open to anyone who joins the call. Most of them could use more people. A lot of that work needs no code at all. Threat models and governance get written in documents and decided in meetings. If you want somewhere to start, pick one working group that matches your interests or role, join a call, and read the notes from previous meetings to get up to speed. Then show up consistently – that part can’t be generated.
That’s also why openness matters beyond community values. Agentic development is not going to run on a single model or a single vendor’s stack. Teams will mix them, and the systems around those agents have to support that choice without losing track of what the agents did or who is accountable for it. That’s the thinking behind JetBrains Air, which we announced the week after the conference.
JetBrains participates in the Agentic AI Foundation because our users will live with the standards worked out in these communities. I still learn more from maintainers in a hallway than anywhere else.
Thank you to Bauke Brenninkmeijer, Michaela Raukar-Herman, and Ruslan Kuleshov for making the meetup happen, to our panelists, to Alex Salkever, Ibrahim Malik, and Jake Pineda for their talks, and to everyone else who came out. We will see you at the next AGNTCon in San Jose. Come find us at our booth.
Meetup photos by Ivan Davletshin
