posts.title: CI/CD Pipeline Observability Tools: How to Choose the Right Setup
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
When a CI/CD pipeline fails, its dashboard can usually show you what went wrong. Pipeline observability tools should help you understand why, whether the cause is a flaky test, an overloaded build agent, or a problem elsewhere in the delivery process.
This becomes harder as pipelines grow more complex. A pipeline touches a lot of separate systems: version control, build agents, containers, test frameworks, artifact repositories, security scanners, and deployment tools. Each one generates its own data, and pulling all of it together during an investigation isn’t easy.
The JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 shows how common these challenges are. When we asked 20,416 respondents about their top three challenges when working with cloud infrastructure, 44% selected debugging and troubleshooting issues in cloud environments.
Security and access control was selected by 36%, as was cost visibility and optimization. Observability was named by 16%, while 12% pointed to having too many separate tools, consoles, or dashboards.
JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Report 2026



This article explains what CI/CD pipeline observability means, which metrics are worth tracking, and how the most common observability tools compare. It also provides a framework for choosing the right CI/CD observability tools for your team.
What is CI/CD pipeline observability?
CI/CD pipeline observability is the ability to understand the state and behavior of a delivery pipeline from the data it produces, including build results, metrics, logs, events, and traces. 
In practical terms, an observable pipeline should help you answer questions such as:
Why are builds taking longer than they did last month? 
Why does one agent pool fail more frequently than another? 
Which pipeline stage introduced a regression? 
Did a code change cause the failure, or did something in the build environment change?
Monitoring and observability are closely related, but they are not identical. Pipeline monitoring tracks known conditions. You define a metric or event, display it on a dashboard, and perhaps create an alert when it crosses a threshold.
Observability helps when the cause of a problem is not immediately clear. It gives you enough connected data to investigate unexpected failures without first adding new tracking and waiting for the issue to occur again.
For example, monitoring can show that build duration has suddenly increased. Observability helps you trace that increase to a particular pipeline, stage, build agent, commit, test, or infrastructure issue.
TeamCity Performance Monitor



What should you observe in a CI/CD pipeline?
Pipeline observability covers both the work performed by the pipeline and the platform running it.
At the pipeline level, these metrics fall into two groups: In the first, we’ve got queue time, total duration, and stage duration, which tell you where developers are kept waiting. In the other group, there are success rates, retries, flaky tests, and cache performance, which tell you where the pipeline itself is becoming less reliable.
At the platform level, teams need visibility into agents or runners, CPU and memory consumption, disk and network activity, server health, and the availability of external dependencies. This context helps distinguish a code problem from an infrastructure problem.
The most useful metrics are those connected to a concrete investigation.

QuestionUseful signalsContext needed
Are developers waiting longer for feedback?Queue time, pipeline duration, stage duration, median and 95th-percentile build durationRepository, branch, pipeline, stage, and agent pool
Are pipelines becoming less reliable?Failure rate, retry rate, canceled runs, flaky-test rateFailure type, test, commit, and environment
Is the build infrastructure keeping up with demand?Agent utilization, available agents, CPU, memory, disk, queue lengthAgent, pool, operating system, and executor type
Is work being repeated unnecessarily?Cache hit rate, artifact reuse, repeated downloadsDependency, cache key, and build configuration
What is driving CI infrastructure cost?Compute time, runner type, concurrency, storage, artifact volumeTeam, project, workload, and cloud resource
Can a failure be tracked back to a change?Commit metadata, configuration changes, and dependency versionsRepository, pull request, and build run





Percentiles are usually more informative than averages for duration and queue-time metrics. A stable average can conceal a poor experience for the slowest 5% or 10% of builds.
Looking only at an overall success rate can hide problems. The number may appear healthy even if one branch, build-agent image, or test suite fails regularly. To find these patterns, teams need to be able to break metrics down by project, branch, pipeline stage, agent pool, environment, and failure type.
Your CI/CD system is normally the best source for run identity and pipeline structure. For example, TeamCity statistic charts connect build duration, queue time, success rates, tests, artifacts, and other statistics to the underlying build configuration. 
This context becomes particularly valuable when CI data is exported to another observability system.
Build configuration statistics in TeamCity



How teams observe CI/CD pipelines in 2026
The State of Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 asked 8,323 respondents which tools they use for CI/CD pipeline observability. Respondents could select more than one answer.
JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Report 2026



Built-in CI/CD dashboards are the most common option, used by 76% of respondents. They are already part of the CI/CD platform, require little setup, and show pipeline runs, stages, tests, and failures in their original context.
However, many teams use more than one observability tool. They might investigate a failed build in the CI/CD dashboard, use Prometheus and Grafana to monitor build infrastructure, and search logs in Elastic or OpenSearch. 
These tools are not direct alternatives: each provides a different type of information. Metrics show trends and changes over time, logs provide detailed records of what happened, and traces show how work moved through different parts of the pipeline.
OpenTelemetry helps collect and send this data, but it still needs a separate system to store and display it.
How to choose a CI/CD pipeline observability tool
Most observability tools promise the same basics: dashboards, alerts, and some integrations. What actually separates them is what data they collect, how well that data stays connected to your pipelines, and how much work it takes to set them up and keep them running.
The following five criteria can help you compare the options and choose the right fit for your team.
1. Investigation depth and CI/CD context
Think about the problems you want the tool to help you investigate. If a pipeline fails, can you quickly find the affected stage or test? Can you compare the failed run with earlier successful ones?
To answer these questions, the tool needs to keep each metric, log, or trace connected to the relevant pipeline run. It should be possible to see which repository, branch, commit, stage, and environment the data came from. 
You may also need information about the pull request, build agent, test, or artifact involved.
TeamCity’s AI Assistant helps analyze failed builds



Built-in CI/CD dashboards are useful because they already have this context. When evaluating an external observability tool, check whether its integration keeps these connections or reduces the pipeline to a collection of unrelated metrics and logs.
2. Correlation across systems
A pipeline problem can come from many places, including a build runner, container, cloud service, artifact repository, external API, or deployment environment.
A good observability tool should connect data from these systems, so that developers do not have to compare timestamps and search through several dashboards to understand what happened. This is especially useful for organizations that work with multiple CI/CD platforms or environments.
According to the State of Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026, 22% of respondents find managing multiple environments challenging, while 12% struggle with having too many separate tools, consoles, or dashboards. An observability tool should bring this information together rather than add another disconnected dashboard.




3. Setup and usability
Different observability tools require different amounts of setup. A built-in CI/CD dashboard may work straight away, while external tools need to be connected to the pipeline and configured to collect, store, and display the right data. Distributed tracing may require additional changes to the pipeline itself.
A more complex setup can be worthwhile if it gives your team the information it needs. However, you should consider how much work the tool will take to introduce and maintain.
The tool should also be easy for developers to use. They are usually the first people to see a pipeline failure. If they cannot understand the data without help from the platform team, the tool will have limited value in everyday investigations.
4. Security and deployment model
The data collected from CI/CD pipelines may include repository and commit details, usernames, infrastructure addresses, and information about build environments. Build logs can also contain passwords, tokens, or other secrets if sensitive information is not properly hidden.
It’s not a small concern, either: Security, permissions, and access control ranked as a top cloud challenge for 36% of survey respondents.
Before choosing a tool, find out where it stores your data, how the data is protected when it is transferred, who can access it, and how long it is kept. Your organization may also need access controls, activity logs, encryption, a choice of data-storage region, or the ability to run the tool on its own infrastructure.
5. Cost, maintenance, and portability
The subscription or license price is only part of the total cost. Collecting large amounts of detailed metrics, logs, and traces can increase storage and processing costs. A self-hosted tool may reduce subscription fees, but your team will still need to provide the infrastructure, install updates, manage backups, and maintain the system.
You should also consider how easy it would be to move your data to another tool. 10% of survey respondents cited vendor lock-in and portability as challenges in using cloud services. 
Open standards cannot make a migration effortless, but they can reduce the amount of data collection and pipeline configuration that must be rebuilt.
Open-source, managed, or a combination?
We often talk about open-source versus commercial platforms as though it’s a binary choice. But most teams have “a foot in both camps”, so to speak.
Prometheus, Grafana, OpenSearch, and OpenTelemetry give you full control over hosting, data, and retention. You decide where it lives and how long it stays. The trade-off is that you’re also the one running and securing it.
Commercial platforms take that job off your hands. You get useful data faster, but you’re paying through subscription and ingestion costs, and you’re trusting someone else with where your data is stored.
Most teams don’t actually pick a side. A typical setup uses OpenTelemetry to collect the data, Prometheus for infrastructure metrics, and a managed platform for storage and analysis on top of both. 
Decide based on what your team already knows how to run and what questions you actually need answered, not based on whether a given platform is open-source or commercial.
CI/CD pipeline observability tools compared
The State of Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 grouped observability tools by type. This means that the results show how widely each approach is taken, but not the usage of individual products. 
For example, 14% use a commercial observability platform, but the survey does not show how this percentage is divided among Datadog, New Relic, and Dynatrace.
For this reason, the comparison below uses the same tool categories as the survey and evaluates each one against our selection framework.
Built-in CI/CD dashboards
Model: Included with a cloud or self-hosted CI/CD platform.
Signals and CI context: Pipeline runs, stages, build logs, tests, changes, queue times, and agent or runner information.
Configuration: Usually available by default, with additional charts, reports, APIs, or metric exports depending on the platform.
Built-in dashboards are generally the best first layer of pipeline observability. A failed test, slow staging, queued builds, and triggering commits are presented as related parts of the same run rather than as separate telemetry records.
Best for: Everyday investigations when most teams use the same CI/CD platform.
Standout capabilities: Strong native CI context, low setup effort, and direct access from the build result.
Limitation: Cross-system visibility is often limited. The dashboard may show that a stage became slower without explaining whether the cause was infrastructure, storage, networking, or an external service.
When evaluating a built-in dashboard, look for historical trends, test history, queue analysis, and agent workload rather than focusing only on the latest run.
TeamCity provides build and project statistics, test histories, logs, agent workload information, and pipeline visualizations. Our article on troubleshooting builds with TeamCity dashboards demonstrates how these sources can be combined during an investigation.
Prometheus and Grafana
Model: Open-source and usually self-managed, with managed Grafana services also available.
Signals and CI context: Time-series metrics, labels, dashboards, and alerts; CI context depends on the exported metrics.
Configuration: Prometheus scrape configuration and alerting rules, usually in YAML; Grafana dashboards and data sources.
A Grafana dashboard of the JetBrains IntelliJ infrastructure team



Prometheus collects and queries time-series data, while Grafana provides dashboards and visualization. Together, they are the most common metrics-based approach in the survey, selected by 29% of respondents.
Best for: Monitoring CI infrastructure, capacity, utilization, and performance trends.
Standout capabilities: Flexible queries and dashboards, strong infrastructure correlation, and control over data storage.
Limitation: Metrics can show where and when behavior changed, but may not contain enough detail to explain the exact cause. Teams must also operate the stack and control metric cardinality.
The quality of the result depends heavily on metric labels. Pipeline, stage, result, project, and agent-pool context make aggregation useful. Individual build IDs and commit hashes should be handled carefully to avoid unnecessarily high cardinality.
TeamCity exposes server metrics in Prometheus format. Our guide to monitoring TeamCity server health with Prometheus and Grafana covers build queues, agents, server load, JVM health, and database connections.
Elastic Stack and OpenSearch
Model: Open-source or open-core software with self-managed and managed deployment options.
Signals and CI context: Primarily logs and searchable events, with support for metrics and traces depending on the stack.
Configuration: Collectors, parsing and ingestion pipelines, schemas, indexes, dashboards, and retention policies
Elastic Stack and OpenSearch represent the log aggregation category, used by 18% of survey respondents. They are useful when an investigation depends on detailed output from pipeline stages, agents, infrastructure, or external services.
Best for: Organizations with log-heavy investigations or an existing centralized logging platform.
Standout capabilities: Search across large volumes of pipeline and infrastructure events.
Limitation: Centralizing logs does not automatically preserve pipeline structure. Ingestion and storage volumes can also become expensive.
Collecting more logs is not enough. Each log entry should show which pipeline run, stage, repository, and build agent it belongs to. Sensitive information in build outputs should also be hidden before the logs are stored.
Elastic documents an OpenTelemetry-based CI/CD observability architecture, while OpenSearch supports the exploration of logs, metrics, and traces. The depth of pipeline context still depends on how the CI/CD system is instrumented.
OpenTelemetry
Model: Open-source, vendor-neutral instrumentation standard; requires a separate backend.
Signals and CI context: Metrics, logs, and traces, with semantic conventions for CI/CD telemetry.
Configuration: Instrumentation or CI integrations, OTLP exporters, and usually an OpenTelemetry Collector.
OpenTelemetry is used by 17% of respondents. It is not a complete observability tool with its own storage and dashboards. Instead, it provides a standard way to collect pipeline data and send it to another observability system.
For example, OpenTelemetry can record a pipeline as a connected sequence of jobs, stages, tests, artifact transfers, and calls to external services. This data can then be stored and analyzed using either an open-source or commercial platform.
Best for: Complex pipelines spanning several tools or services, particularly when portability matters.
Standout capabilities: Cross-system tracing and vendor-neutral collection of metrics, logs, and traces.
Limitation: OpenTelemetry does not provide storage, dashboards, or a finished investigation experience. Instrumentation can require significant work.
The OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for CI/CD cover spans, metrics, and logs. The OpenTelemetry Collector can process and route those signals to one or more backends.
When evaluating this approach, check which parts of the pipeline are instrumented automatically. A trace containing only pipeline and job names may add little beyond the native CI/CD interface. Its value grows when it connects pipeline activity to processes, agents, network calls, or deployment systems.
Commercial observability platforms
Model: Primarily managed SaaS, with data-collection and hosting options varying by vendor.
Signals and CI context: Metrics, logs, traces, events, tests, and pipeline data, depending on the integration.
Configuration: Native integrations, agents, plugins, APIs, or OpenTelemetry collectors.
Commercial observability platforms were selected by 14% of respondents. The survey grouped Datadog, New Relic, and Dynatrace together, so this figure should not be interpreted as individual adoption data for any of them.
Best for: Organizations already using a commercial observability platform that want to add CI/CD data to the same environment.
Standout capabilities: Managed storage and analysis, cross-system correlation, vendor support, and ready-made integrations.
Limitation: Subscription, ingestion, and retention costs can grow with verbose logs and test data. CI/CD integration depth, portability, and data residency vary by vendor.
The evaluation should focus on the specific CI/CD integration rather than the platform’s general feature list. Test whether users can move from a pipeline regression to the relevant stage, test, log, agent metric, and commit without manually rebuilding that context.
For example, Datadog Pipeline Visibility provides pipeline-level data for supported CI providers, while New Relic can receive CI/CD information through integrations and change tracking. 
TeamCity users can also connect build data to Datadog CI Visibility when Datadog is already part of their observability stack.
Custom in-house observability
Model: Usually self-hosted and developed internally.
Signals and CI context: Defined by the organization, from normalized pipeline events to custom cost and infrastructure data.
Configuration: Custom collectors, APIs, schemas, storage, dashboards, and access controls.
Twelve percent of respondents use a custom solution. This approach is more common when an organization operates several CI/CD systems, proprietary infrastructure, unusual hardware, or delivery processes that general-purpose tools do not model well.
Best for: Large or specialized organizations whose requirements cannot be met through existing integrations.
Standout capabilities: Complete control over the data model, hosting, CI context, and organization-specific analysis.
Limitation: The organization owns the entire lifecycle, including instrumentation, security, upgrades, documentation, and user experience.
Teams usually do not need to build an entire observability system from scratch. They can use existing tools to collect and store pipeline data, then build only the custom reports and features their organization needs.
How to evaluate the options for pipeline observability
Most teams do not need a single tool to handle every part of pipeline observability.
Start with the dashboard built into your CI/CD platform. If you need more information about build queues, available agents, or server health, add a metrics tool. If you need to search detailed information from several systems, collect the relevant logs in one place. Tracing is most useful when you need to follow what happens inside complex pipelines and external services.
When comparing tools, test them using problems your team has actually faced, such as a slow build, a flaky test, or an overloaded build agent. Check how quickly a developer can find the affected pipeline run, understand where the problem occurred, and gather enough evidence to explain it.
Also consider the work needed to set up and maintain each tool, as well as the amount of data it will store. Estimate the cost using a typical month of pipeline activity rather than a small test project.
Choose a tool that helps your team understand and resolve pipeline problems quickly without adding unnecessary complexity.
Final thoughts
An effective pipeline observability setup keeps information from different parts of the delivery process connected. This allows teams to see which commit triggered a build, which agent ran a stage, and whether a slowdown was related to the available infrastructure.
Start with the questions your current setup cannot answer. Use the framework in this article to identify which capabilities are missing, then test potential tools using real pipeline problems and typical data volumes. 
The right setup should help your team understand what happened and find the cause more quickly.

posts.title: Python vs Go: A Practical Comparison for Developers
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Two things are true about Python: It’s the most popular programming language in the world, and it’s the most common companion language for Go developers. How do we know that? From the Developer Ecosystem 2026 survey by JetBrains.
But we also know a lot more about the developers who use these two languages – both from quantitative data from different surveys, as well as qualitative data from our interviews with professionals who switched from Python to Go.
In this article, we share findings from these sources, going well beyond the simple syntax comparisons you will usually find. We will look at how the two languages differ, what the surveys tell us about the people who use them, and what our interviews say about the trade-offs between Python and Go, so that if you’re considering making the leap, you don’t have to dive in blind.
TL;DR
The article compares Python and Go across language design, performance, tooling, developer profiles, and migration experiences.
Python favors expressive code and rapid iteration; Go favors explicit, standardized code that is easy to maintain across teams.
Go excels in raw performance and concurrency, and is widely used in cloud infrastructure. Python remains stronger for machine learning, data science, and scientific computing.
Go developers are typically more infrastructure-focused and more senior. Go is rarely someone’s first language, whereas Python is very beginner-friendly.
Python leads in building AI models, yet Go developers create AI integrations at nearly the same rate: 46% vs 44%.
Moving to Go rarely means abandoning Python. Most teams use both, with Go for services and infrastructure and Python for AI and data workloads.
A note about the data
Unless stated otherwise, all survey figures come from the JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 (28,945 responses, fielded May–July 2026). We compare two groups: developers who selected Go among their primary languages (1,836) and developers who selected Python (11,298). The groups overlap, with 619 respondents selecting both languages. Therefore, every gap below is a conservative estimate of the real difference. Some questions were shown to only a part of each group, so bases are provided for reference. The qualitative material comes from interviews with developers who moved production workloads from Python to Go. We conducted the interviews between April and May 2026 and included seven participants who began using Go within the past year.
Python vs Go – languages compared
Core philosophy
On paper, Python and Go sound like they’d get along. Python lays out the core principles in the Zen of Python: Simple is better than complex, readability counts, there should be one obvious way to do it, etc. Go, as per Effective Go, “focuses on simplicity, reliability, and efficiency”, and is “specifically designed to make it easy to build software at scale”.
In practice, Python often optimizes for the person writing the code, offering multiple ways to say the same thing. Go optimizes for the person (or, nowadays, possibly the agent) reading someone else’s code two years later, so it picks one way to say most things and makes you spell it out. The goal is for all Go code to look like other Go code.
We point this out right at the beginning, because however similar these two philosophies look, this difference in approach underlies almost all the other language design differences that follow.
Ease of use and learning curve
Python is arguably one of the easiest programming languages to learn among those widely used in production. The syntax resembles natural language, the core set of constructs is small, and beginners can focus on programming ideas instead of language mechanics, leading to less frustration and faster results. Surveys consistently show Python to be one of the most popular programming languages (if not the most popular). In 2026, 10% of Python developers have been coding for less than a year, 23% are students or working students, and 19% hold junior positions, showing the language has a strong early-stage user base.
Python’s popularity among early learners is almost self-perpetuating. Initially, the language was well-suited to introductory courses and learning materials largely because it lets beginners print “Hello, world” with little ceremony, bypassing much boring theory in favor of real outputs. It also has the added benefit of being a generalist language that can handle a variety of use cases. Later, the sheer number of introductory courses and learning materials made it a natural choice for anyone who wanted to pick up programming but didn’t know where to start.
It’s not the same case with Go. In fact, you would be hard-pressed to find courses that teach you programming through Go. There are two reasons for that. First, Go 1.0 was released in 2012, long after Python had already become firmly embedded in CS curricula. The other is that Go solves problems that beginners don’t have. Explicit error handling, static types, and interfaces, which we’ll discuss later, all pay off across a large codebase maintained by a team over years. Go also has a much narrower set of implementations than Python, which makes it even less appealing for beginners.
That said, Go was also designed to be easy to learn, but for a different reason: Any large team should be able to onboard a new engineer quickly. Many Go developers will say that if you already know general programming concepts, you can become productive in Go in a matter of days or weeks. Developers we talked to said that Go “feels as easy to write as Python” and that it “strikes a good balance between Python’s simplicity and Java’s explicit nature”.
Syntax and readability
When you read Python, you can often follow it even without programming experience, because it reads relatively close to English. Python is dynamically typed, so type declarations are optional, though in practice, many companies and large codebases now write Python with type hints throughout, checked by tools like mypy or Pyright. Most of the ecosystem follows the formatting conventions set out in PEP 8, but they are still optional, and so some teams diverge from them.
Go, by contrast, is explicit and deliberately limited, which contributes to the cross-team readability we mentioned. It is statically typed, which makes it noticeably more verbose than Python. That was the main syntactic complaint raised by the developers we interviewed. Formatting in Go is not a matter of preference: gofmt will shape your code into the canonical form, whether you like the conventions or not.
One syntactic difference that developers consistently pointed out as a big adjustment when moving from Python to Go was error handling. Python lets you push failure handling to the edges of a function with try / except. Experienced Go developers clutch their pearls at the sight of that.
# Python: handle failure where it is convenient
try:
    profile = get_user(user_id)
except UserNotFound:
    return render_404()
// Go: handle failure where it happens
profile, err := getUser(userID)
if err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, ErrUserNotFound) {
        return render404(w)
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("get user %s: %w", userID, err)
}
The Go version is longer, and in a large handler, developers will find themselves writing the if err != nil boilerplate ad nauseam. In return, they get control flow with no invisible jumps: Every path a value can take is explicit. Both approaches come with trade-offs.
Type system
Python’s dynamic typing checks types at runtime. This gives developers flexibility in writing and can speed up iteration, but it also means some type errors only show up when the code runs. The flexibility extends to the object model, which relies on duck typing: The code cares less about what an object is than what it can do. The developers we interviewed said they sorely missed duck typing, as it makes testing and mocking more difficult in Go.
Go checks types before the program runs. This results in fewer type-related failures reaching production and makes refactoring safer, but also causes code verbosity, as we touched on earlier.
Object model and polymorphism
Python is object-oriented in the way that most developers first learn the term. Everything is an object, and classes inherit from other classes (several at once, if you insist). Polymorphism works in two ways: down the class hierarchy when a subclass overrides its parent’s method, and sideways through duck typing, where anything with a read() method can be handed to code that expects a file.
Go has none of that hierarchy. There are no classes, no inheritance, and no way to declare that one type is a subtype of another. Instead, structs have methods attached to them, as well as interfaces that types satisfy implicitly without ever naming them.
# Python: the implementation announces its role
class Store(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def get(self, key: str) -> bytes: ...

class RedisStore(Store):
    def get(self, key: str) -> bytes:
        ...
// Go: the consumer declares what it needs; RedisStore never mentions Getter
type Getter interface {
    Get(key string) ([]byte, error)
}

func handleRead(g Getter, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    return g.Get(key)
}
Notice how the dependency runs. In Python, RedisStore inherits from Store, so the abstraction sits with the implementation. In Go, handleRead declares the one method it actually calls, and RedisStore never learns that Getter exists. That’s why Go developers say to “accept interfaces, return structs”, and that’s why interfaces stay small – io.Reader and io.Writer have a single method each.
Performance and speed
Go follows a traditional compilation model, producing a native binary. Python, on the other hand, takes a hybrid approach: Source code is compiled to bytecode, which the interpreter then executes.
As most compiled languages do, Go wins in terms of raw speed. You can compare the patterns across latency, throughput, and startup time on The Computer Language Benchmarks Game. Microbenchmarks like these don’t really translate directly to real workloads, and we wouldn’t be surprised if you made nothing of them. Our interviewees told us what the difference meant in production for them: One team migrated to Go after cold starts on AWS Lambda in Python exceeded 10 seconds; another measured a tenfold improvement in request times after rewriting their Python service in Go.
But raw language speed matters only when your service is actually compute-bound or latency-sensitive, and plenty of services are neither. Equally importantly, the Python interpreter is not slow where it counts most for one of its largest user bases. In machine learning, data work, and numerical computing, libraries like NumPy and PyTorch offload expensive operations to optimized native code, making interpreter overhead much less relevant. When we asked migrating developers where they decided to keep Python code, they confidently listed all AI and ML workflows – LLMs, chatbots, RAGs, and model training.
Memory management
Memory management is another important part of the performance discussion. Both languages manage memory for you, but differently: Go uses a tracing garbage collector, while CPython uses reference counting alongside a cyclic garbage collector. This affects what developers can fine-tune and what they need to design around.
Go’s GC runs concurrently with the program and is designed to minimize stop-the-world pauses. Developers can tune this behavior: GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT set the pacing, and the memory profile (heap and allocs) tells you when a service allocates too hard.
In CPython, an object is typically freed the moment its last reference disappears. Memory use is predictable, and pauses are rarely worth measuring, but the cost is spread across every operation, and there’s little to room tune it.   
Concurrency and parallelism
Even though both languages support concurrency, developers we talked to cited better concurrency as the reason why they switched from Python to Go.
Goroutines are central to Go’s design. They are lightweight threads managed by the runtime. They are cheap to create, carry little overhead, and scale to thousands of concurrent operations. The runtime handles the scheduling, which makes the model simpler than in Python – there is no separate async/await syntax, so a function is just a function. However, if you start to spawn goroutines without controlling their lifecycle, you’d better be ready to deal with race conditions, leaks, and deadlocks before long.
The other half of the concurrency model in Go are channels – typed conduits that pass values between goroutines and synchronize them. Instead of guarding shared state with a lock, Go can pass the value to whichever needs it next. A select statement waits on several channels at once, which is how Go expresses timeouts, cancellation, and fan-in using built-in language constructs. These very same primitives also produce common Go bugs: goroutine leaks and more deadlocks. 
Meanwhile, Python relies on standard libraries, single-threaded event loops, and sub-processes to work around interpreter constraints. It offers threading, but in CPython, the global interpreter lock (GIL) has historically prevented threads from running Python bytecode simultaneously, making it ineffective for CPU-bound parallelism. For I/O-bound concurrency, there is asyncio, and for real parallelism there is multiprocessing, but that adds memory overhead and requires inter-process communication.
It’s worth noting that the GIL itself is no longer a necessity – starting with Python 3.13, PEP 703 introduced an officially supported free-threaded build, and 3.14 continues that work. Most production code still runs with the GIL in place, but with each new release, the claim that “Python can’t do real threading” is becoming less true.
# Python: async/await, and the coloring that comes with it
async def fetch_all(urls):
    return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))
// Go: ordinary functions run concurrently
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for _, u := range urls {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        fetch(u)
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
The approach to concurrency gives Go much of its practical advantage in high-throughput services, and having experienced both, our interviewees praised Go for being “async by default” and better suited for high-concurrency components, and they described it as having a superior concurrency model that’s highly performant and appealing for real-world use cases.
Libraries, frameworks, and IDEs
Go’s self-contained ecosystem
Go was never built as just a programming language, but as an ecosystem. As the Go team puts it, the goal was “an end-to-end platform with tooling all around the software development lifecycle” (Google for Developers), with formatters, test frameworks, dependency management, and security tools included in the toolchain, alongside a standard library that’s comprehensive enough to make external frameworks optional, if not irrelevant.
The Developer Ecosystem 2026 survey shows how successful the Go team has been in achieving that goal. For example, among Gophers, the standard html/template and text/template library packages are used by 31% and 22% of developers respectively, whereas the only other significant alternative – templ – is used by 11%.
Almost half of Gophers either don’t write unit tests or don’t use testing frameworks: 14% don’t write unit tests at all, and 35% don’t use frameworks for testing – the testing package provides everything they need in that regard. Others may also reach for tools such as Testify (31%) or GoMock (25%). The remaining libraries are far less popular.
For web development, 46% of developers use the standard net/http library, compared to 48% who use Gin. This proves that where a third-party framework exists, it doesn’t compete with the many other frameworks, but only with the standard library. Oftentimes, it loses.

Python’s broad ecosystem
Python’s ecosystem works the other way around. The Python Package Index (PyPI) is vast and mature, and where the standard library stops, several strong alternatives tend to compete.

The data science landscape is more fragmented, and developers use those libraries simultaneously: 69% use NumPy, 68% use pandas, 50% use PyTorch, 49% use Matplotlib, etc. With Python, there’s often no clear leader, and choosing the right framework or library is part of the job.

One reason is how much of Go’s surrounding ecosystem developers can access without having to assemble it themselves. GoLand installs with a test runner, debugger, coverage, and profilers wired into the toolchain. The analysis runs across the whole project, rather than only the open file. Interprocedural nil checks and unhandled-error inspections can catch the mistakes a Python developer might otherwise only see at runtime. Suffice it to say, Alan Donovan of the Go team has also described traditional IDEs like ours as setting “the gold standard” for refactoring because of their tight integration between the analysis logic and the user interface.

The Python side is more fragmented and has more Python-specific options, such as Jupyter Notebook and, of course, PyCharm. The latter is used by 30% of Python developers (PyCharm – 22%, PyCharm Pro – 8%), with VS Code at 41%. Notebooks explain much of the fragmentation, since data and service work don’t necessarily require the same toolset. Whatever you build in Python, PyCharm has first-class support for your stack, your frameworks, and your workflow – for web, data, and ML workflows – with notebooks running alongside a debugger and type checker. It parses your code and resolves usages, types, and dependencies throughout your entire project. So you always know exactly what your code does and what will break if it changes, for you and your agents alike.
Try PyCharm
                                                    
If you use both Go and Python – as a quarter of Gophers do – it’s worth noting that both GoLand and PyCharm are built on the same platform, so keymaps, shortcuts, and settings sync between them. GoLand also supports Python functionalities through the Python Community Edition plugin.
Python vs Go – broader landscapes
The language itself is one thing, but many other factors go into deciding which language you choose to work with. Developers consider what the languages are used for, who uses them, and how they’re maintained. In this section, we’ll provide insights on the factors that shape the broader landscapes of Python and Go.
Go developers are more senior
Across all questions about age, experience, and seniority in the Developer Ecosystem 2026 survey, Gophers tend to be further along in their career than Python developers.
On overall professional coding experience (not just experience in their main programming language), 20% of Go devs report 16 years or more, compared to 12% among Python developers. At the other end, 9% of Gophers have 1–2 years of experience, compared to 20% of Python developers.
Most Go professionals have senior roles, at 60%, with only 2% being trainees and 10% juniors. Meanwhile, 42% of Python professionals are seniors; trainees (6%) and juniors (19%) make up a quarter of the cohort.
72% of Go developers are employed full-time, compared to 51% of Python developers. Students and working students make up 8% of Gophers, compared to 23% of the Python population.
Finally, by age, the largest group of Go developers is aged 30–34 (23%), compared to Python’s largest group, aged 21–24 (22%).
These differences align with the point we made earlier: Python is a very popular first language for learners, while Go is almost never chosen as a first language and instead is picked up by more experienced developers later in their careers.
It’s important to keep this in mind as you read the following sections on developer demographics, because a lot of these numbers may look like differences between two languages, where in reality, they’re just differences between a senior population vs a general one that you would see regardless of what ecosystems you compare.

In other words, learning Go itself will not guarantee you a higher salary, but the roles that require Go generally pay better.
What they build
The Developer Ecosystem survey also asks people what functionality their code implements.
Go developers more frequently reported:
69% – providing APIs and services (Python – 41%)
63% – integrating with APIs and services (Python – 47%)
51% – application logic and workflows (Python – 37%)
47% – user interface (Python – 41%)
35% – libraries and frameworks (Python – 26%)
Meanwhile, Python developers reported higher rates for:
38% – data processing and analytics (Go – 30%)
36% – artificial intelligence and machine learning (Go – 20%)
32% – data science and data analytics (Go – 15%)
The question of where their code is executed adds more context: A vast majority of Go developers target server, infrastructure, or cloud environments (74% compared to 57% of Python developers. On the other hand, 66% of Python developers target the desktop (Go – 47%).
Python is clearly a general-purpose language with a stronghold in AI, ML, and data work that favors local execution, while Go is heavily oriented towards networked services and infrastructure.
There is, however, a particularly interesting line item in the set: integration with AI. While AI development per se is a Python domain, integrations are not. 46% of Go developers report implementing AI integrations, against Python’s 44%, almost equal numbers. Asked about the types of development they do at work, 51% of Python developers reported working with AI and AI tools, compared to Go’s 48%. Go engineers may not train the models, but they are building AI-powered products at roughly the same rate as Python developers.

DevOps: Same job, different toolbox
One other point of convergence between Python and Go developers that deserves its own section is DevOps. Both groups are involved in that area, though Python developers (31%) somewhat less than Gophers (45%). The two groups also tend to use different tools.
For orchestration, Go developers are more likely to use tooling overall, and especially Kubernetes. Only 8% of Go developers don’t use container orchestration tools (compared to 17% for Python); 58% use Kubernetes (compared to 39%). The engineers we talked to cited Go’s deep integration with Kubernetes as one of the reasons they migrate entire services from Python to Go.
For configuration management, Terraform leads both groups. However, Python developers lean more toward cloud-native IaC tools (29% for Python, 23% for Go) or use nothing (21% for Python, 15% for Go), while Go developers choose GitOps more often (27% for Go, 21% for Python).
When it comes to DevOps practices, Go developers report using them more often overall, with one exception: AI-driven operations (12% of Go developers and 18% of Python developers). Python developers are also more likely to use no DevOps practices at all (6% for Python, 2% for Go).
So even if you move from Python to Go in the same type of role, the toolset change might be as big an adjustment as the language change itself.

Operating systems
A curious difference surfaced when we asked developers about the operating system they use for their development environment. Go developers work on macOS (70%) and Linux (57%) significantly more than on Windows (44%). Meanwhile, Python developers use Windows first (66%), then split almost evenly between macOS (54%) and Linux (52%).
For developers planning to migrate to Go, sticking with Windows doesn’t have to complicate deployment, even when the target is a Linux server. For pure Go, building a Linux binary from any of the three operating systems takes no more than two environment variables, while a Python deployment still has to find a matching interpreter and native packages, wherever it ends up.

Two different approaches to AI
We’ve already discussed using Python and Go for AI development, but what about using AI for Go and Python development? Both groups use AI heavily at work, but there’s a difference in how and what they use it for.
Go developers report using AI daily for tasks such as editing code across multiple files (60% vs 52%), agentic development of features or programs (51% vs 41%),  generating commit messages (51% vs 36%) and tests (47% vs 34%), or performing code reviews (39% vs 34%).
Meanwhile, Python developers lead on one task: learning new things about coding and software development (38% of Python developers vs 31% of Go developers), which is consistent with earlier data showing a larger early-career population among Python developers.
There is, however, a long list of tasks where the two groups are indistinguishable: refactoring, debugging, checking code for potential issues, asking general questions, or generating boilerplate – even though you’d expect Go developers to jump on the last one much more, considering the verbosity of the language.

So AI-assisted coding is common in both ecosystems. Go developers have simply wired it into the production chores of a maintenance-heavy codebase: commits, tests, reviews, and multi-file edits.
The groups also tend to use different tools. Go developers are more likely to use terminal and agentic tools like Claude Code (45% vs 40%), OpenAI Codex (24% vs 17%), Cursor (17% vs 12%), and OpenCode (12% vs 6%). Python developers, in turn, reach more for general-purpose assistants and Google or Microsoft surfaces like ChatGPT (20% vs 16%), Google Antigravity (9% vs 5%), and Microsoft 365 Copilot (4% vs 1%).

Transitioning from Python to Go
One-way path well traveled
You may ask why we’re focusing on transitioning from Python to Go, not the other way around. The data leaves little doubt about the path developers are taking. Python is already the most common second language among Go developers – 35% of Gophers declare it as their other primary language. But most Go developers (70%) say they have no intention of adopting another language in the next 12 months, and if they do, they name Rust (16%), rather than Python (2%). On the other hand, 10% of Python developers (a much larger cohort in terms of absolute numbers) plan to pick up Go, roughly 5.5 times the rate at which Go developers plan to pick up Python.

Multiple answers allowed. n/a: respondents already use this language as a primary one. * Statistically significant difference (p < 0.05, adjusted).
Why make the switch from Python to Go?
Despite working in different roles and on different products, the developers we interviewed gave consistent reasons for transitioning from Python to Go. These were:
Better performance and speed, including cold starts, latency, and operating cost.
Easier and more effective concurrency model.
Type safety that catches failures that would otherwise reach production at compile time.
Proximity to the platform, since Kubernetes and much of the cloud-native toolchain are written in Go, so teams working on that infrastructure already interact with Go daily.
What they gained and what they lost
Perceived potential gains are one thing, but did Go actually deliver? According to the developers we interviewed, it did in the areas described above. But they also found benefits they weren’t expecting: predictable formatting and linting that contributed to “clean code”, out-of-the-box tooling, and simplicity comparable to Python’s.
But Go also has flaws that are obvious to developers coming from Python. Just like the reasons for adopting Go were consistent, so were the complaints:
Explicit error handling that’s fundamentally different from Python, less intuitive, and more repetitive.
Overall verbosity and opinionatedness, with more lines needed to convey the same behavior and fewer ways to express it.
An object model that makes testing and mocking noticeably more difficult.
Library gaps, especially for testing.
Did they really leave?
“Migrating”, “transitioning”, and “switching over” may all sound like final decisions to leave Python behind, but that’s not really the case. Not one of the developers we interviewed removed Python from their stack completely. They kept it for artificial intelligence and machine learning, data science, and pipelines on platforms that only support Python, as well as simply because they work on larger teams that already know Python and are productive in it.
The realistic outcome of “moving to Go” is not becoming a monoglot, but having a polyglot codebase where each language is used for what it’s best suited for.
Conclusions
So, which language should you choose? Is it worth dropping Python in favor of Go? We hope that by now the answer is clear – it’s not a matter of which language is better, but which one is a better fit. Based on our data and developer testimony, here’s what we found.
Go may be a better fit if:
Performance is crucial for your app: Latency, throughput, or cold starts are problems you actually have and can measure.
The workload is concurrent, especially if it is I/O-heavy.
The service is long-lived and maintained by a team, not one person.
The system already depends heavily on Kubernetes and the rest of the cloud-native toolchain.
Python may be a better fit if:
The work is machine learning, data science, or numerical computing.
Your platform only accepts Python, as managed ETL and notebook environments frequently do.
Iteration speed matters more than runtime speed, which is often the case for internal tooling and prototypes.
The library you depend on has no Go equivalent; for a lot of the scientific stack, there isn’t one.
Language features alone rarely determine the best choice. When deciding what to build with, the teams weigh in the toolchain they already run, the languages their colleagues already know or are willing to learn, and how much of the existing system they are willing to change. Those things carry more weight than any benchmark, and they are why developers we talked to ended up using both languages, instead of choosing one.
Frequently asked questions
Can Go replace Python completely?
For a lot of backend work, yes, in principle. In practice, it doesn’t. None of the developers we interviewed removed Python from their stack completely. They kept it for machine learning and data science, for pipelines on platforms that only accept Python, and because the teams around them already know it. In the Developer Ecosystem 2026 survey, about a quarter of Go developers report using Python in the same project.
Is Go good for data engineering?
It depends on which end of the pipeline you mean. Go works well for moving data around, including ingestion services, stream processing, API integrations, and CLI tooling, and 30% of Go developers report working on data processing and analytics, compared with Python’s 38%. The analytical end is a different story: Only 15% of Gophers do data science and data analytics, against 32% of Python developers, and the library ecosystem reflects that.
How long does it take a Python developer to learn Go?
Days to weeks for the language itself. The syntax is small, gofmt settles the formatting arguments, and developers we talked to said Go “feels as easy to write as Python”. What takes longer is everything around it: system concepts such as pointers, interfaces, goroutines, and channels, as well as the habits Go asks you to change, from explicit error handling to designing test seams instead of patching at runtime.
The bigger adjustment may not be the language after all. Go work tends to sit closer to Kubernetes, Terraform, and GitOps, so if you’re moving into a Go team from a Python one, budget as much time for learning the toolchain as for the syntax.
Is Go good for machine learning?
For training models, probably not. 20% of Go developers work on artificial intelligence and machine learning, against 36% of Python developers, and the developers we interviewed were blunt about why: Python has the libraries, while Go lacks equivalents.
When it comes to building products around the models, it’s a different story. 46% of Go developers implement AI integrations, against Python’s 44% – a negligible difference. Gophers generally aren’t training the models, but they sure are serving them.
Can Go and Python be used in the same project?
Not only can they be used together, they often are. 27% of Go developers report using Python alongside Go in the same project, behind TypeScript (43%) and just ahead of JavaScript (24%). We know from interviews that the usual division of labor follows each language’s strengths: Go for the networked services and infrastructure, Python for data work, machine learning, and anything that depends on the scientific library stack.

posts.title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals.

By: Wendy Ran Wei, Hao Li, Weiwei Guo, Xiaowei Liu, Xueyin Chen, Chun How Tan, Malay Haldar, Soumyadip Banerjee, Kedar Bellare, Huiji Gao, Sanjeev Katariya, and Stephanie Moyerman
Introduction
Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search.
Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. Promptagator [2] improves query diversity using few-shot examples, but is still limited by the gap between its generation distribution and real user behavior.
In this post, we describe Contrastive And Seed-guided Training for natural Language sEarch (CASTLE), our framework for jointly generating queries and producing relevance labels from Airbnb’s own de-identified booking data. Our paper describing CASTLE was accepted as a full research paper at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management, more widely known as CIKM 2026 [3].
Challenges
Generating useful synthetic training data for search requires more than producing grammatically plausible queries. The distribution of synthetic queries must match how real guests actually search; their preferred phrasing, query length, and attributes they tend to mention. If queries fail to match real-world search patterns, the model trained on them will generalize poorly.
We measured this mismatch using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (a measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution) between synthetic and real query distributions — both over surface-level query statistics and over attribute types (property type, amenity, location, and so on). Prior approaches scored between 9.33 and 26.2 on the KL divergence metric: far from the real-user distribution. Beyond distributional alignment, we also needed relevance labels. Generating a query is only half the problem; knowing which listings are relevant to it is the other half.
Solution
CASTLE addresses both challenges through a single mechanism: contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions, selected in accordance with user privacy permissions. When a guest books a specific listing after viewing several possible alternatives, that event implicitly encodes preference: the booked listing was selected over the others. We use these (positive, negative) pairs of listings — where the negative is randomly sampled from the other viewed-but-not-booked alternatives — as the structured input for query generation. Listing features include amenities, property details, and a one sentence summary of recent public guest reviews, with personal identifying information removed. Because we instruct the LLM to generate a query that is satisfied by the positive listing but not the negative, the relevance label is correct by construction; no post-hoc judgment is required. Crucially, what is “positive” and “negative” is determined by actual, previous user booking behavior, not by the LLM itself, so there is no circularity in the subsequent generation of relevance labels.
CASTLE architecture overview — contrastive listing pairs feeding into seed-guided query generation
Query generation. We combine three prompt variants to maximize coverage and realism. Template-based prompts ensure structural diversity across common query patterns. Few-shot prompts use approximately 500 seed queries collected from targeted user research as linguistic exemplars, grounding generated queries in authentic guest language. Attribute-grounded prompts focus the query on specific distinguishing attributes between the two listings, such as a fireplace or proximity to a ski resort. An explicit variety mechanism encourages the model to vary query length and phrasing across samples, preventing “query collapse,” where an unconditioned LLM converges on the same short phrase repeatedly.
Together, these variants produce a word-count distribution with standard deviation σ = 2.48, closely matching real users (σ = 2.49), compared to σ = 0.99 from baselines (InPars and Promptagator) without the seed-guided mechanism. It is worth noting that real Airbnb guests tend to search with concise, intent-focused phrases, typically four to eight words, rather than long natural-language sentences. CASTLE is designed to match this real-world distribution, not to generate artificially verbose queries.
Query length distribution comparison — CASTLE vs. baselines vs. real users
Flexible input design. For listing pairs where contrastive grounding is not available, such as newly listed properties with no booking history, we supplement with a Virtual Judge (VJ), an LLM evaluator that assigns relevance labels to additional query–listing pairs. This extends coverage to long-tail intents without sacrificing the quality guarantees of the contrastive construction for the core training set. We also introduce a real-query seed variant, CASTLE-R, designed for production settings where some real traffic has begun to accumulate.
Results
We evaluate CASTLE against two previous approaches, InPars-style generation and Promptagator, on two axes: query distributional alignment and label quality.
On KL divergence against real user queries, CASTLE achieves 1.01 — a 9.2× improvement over the best baseline (Promptagator at 9.33). The improvement holds at the attribute-type level as well: CASTLE’s attribute-type KL of 0.08 is lower than even our hand-curated survey seed queries (0.09), meaning the generated queries capture the diversity of real guest intents more faithfully than the seeds themselves.
KL divergence comparison across methods — CASTLE vs. baselines vs. real user distribution
To validate label quality, we conducted a human evaluation with three independent subject matter experts reviewing 200 sampled triplets. Annotators agreed with CASTLE’s relevance assignments at 91–93% across all three raters, confirming that the contrastive construction produces high-quality relevance labels without any human annotation in the loop.
Beyond cold-start, CASTLE’s synthetic data continues to provide value once real traffic accumulates. Because generation is conditioned on specific listing characteristics, it naturally oversamples long-tail intents that appear rarely in organic traffic, such as property types or amenity combinations that guests only search for occasionally, but that have high importance when they do appear.
Conclusion
The key insight in CASTLE is that authentic booking behavior and LLM generation are complementary, not competing. Contrastive listing pairs from booking sessions ground query generation in real platform behavior and provide relevance labels by construction, while LLM prompting provides the query diversity and linguistic variety that behavioral data alone cannot supply. Together, they close the gap between synthetic and real user distributions in a way that neither approach achieves independently.
Looking ahead, we are exploring multi-turn conversational search, where a guest might begin with “cabin near skiing” and refine to “one that allows dogs” — a setting in which cold-start data generation is an even harder problem, and where the contrastive grounding approach may generalize further. For the full technical treatment, see our CIKM 2026 paper at arxiv.org/abs/2605.21812 (DOI: 10.1145/3799682.3841071).
Interested in tackling these kinds of challenges? Browse our previous publications or explore our open roles.
Acknowledgments
We would like to thank our collaborators across the AI Platform — Relevance & Personalization team for their support throughout this project.
References
[1] Jeronymo, Vitor, et al. “InPars-v2: Large Language Models as Efficient Dataset Generators for Information Retrieval.” arXiv:2301.01820, 2023.
[2] Dai, Zhuyun, et al. “Promptagator: Few-shot Dense Retrieval From 8 Examples.” ICLR, 2023.
[3] Wei, Wendy Ran, et al. “CASTLE: Contrastive and Seed-Guided Training for Cold-Start Natural Language Search.” ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 2026. DOI: 10.1145/3799682.3841071.

posts.title: Stop waiting on a failed build
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
A project fails to compile, but the solution build keeps going. You already have an error to fix, while other projects continue using build time to tell you the solution still doesn’t build.
Visual Studio 2026 version 18.11 adds an opt-in way to stop a solution build after the first project failure. If your next step is to fix that failure and try again, you can make the build stop there too.
Choose when the build should stop
Open Tools > Options > Projects and Solutions > Build and Run and enable Stop solution build after first failure.
When a project fails, Visual Studio stops starting queued projects and safely stops projects already building. It still reports the build as failed, not canceled. You don’t have to watch for the first error and manually cancel the remaining work.
This stops the solution build, not only the projects that depend on the failed project. That’s an important choice: you get back to the first problem sooner, but you don’t collect the results of every remaining project in that build.
If you prefer to see those results before you start fixing errors, leave the setting disabled. That preserves the existing behavior. You can also turn it off again on the same settings page.
Measure the wait after a failure
In four test builds, post-failure completion time averaged 26 seconds with the setting disabled and 1.5 seconds with it enabled. That’s about a 94% reduction in the wait after a failure, not a claim that successful builds run 94% faster.

Your results depend on the solution and where a failure occurs. A solution with a long dependency chain or substantial parallel work can have more remaining work to stop than a small solution that finishes almost immediately anyway.
The Developer Community request describes a concrete version of this problem: a packaging project kept trying to build even after a dependency failed. The new option gives you a solution-wide stopping policy rather than requiring you to interrupt the build yourself.
Keep the two decisions separate
This setting answers when should a failed build stop? It doesn’t decide which projects you build in the first place. Existing Build and Run options cover choices such as building only startup projects and dependencies when you run or debug.
Try stop-on-failure on a solution where you normally cancel the build after seeing an error. Compare that post-failure wait, then keep the policy that fits how you troubleshoot.

posts.title: New Tools, New Workflows and the Value of the Visual Studio Subscription: What We Learned at VSLive! San Diego
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
What happens when developers who have spent decades working with Visual Studio start rethinking how they write code, learn new skills, and expand their access to development tools? 
At VSLive! San Diego, we had an opportunity to find out as developers gathered for five days of technical sessions, hands-on learning, and conversations about Visual Studio, .NET, AI, cloud, data, and modern application development.  
One of the most interesting things we heard in San Diego was how readily experienced developers are adopting new tools and workflows. 
GitHub Copilot is part of that story, and developers aren’t limiting themselves to a single AI experience. They’re building broader, more differentiated tool kits. But they aren’t necessarily replacing familiar tools. They’re expanding how they work, choosing different experiences depending on the task, and finding new ways to solve problems.  
This is why events like VSLive! provide such an amazing opportunity for developers tackling these kinds of changes. Not only do they get to learn from expert led sessions and hands on labs, they get to learn from each other. 
AI is changing how developers approach unfamiliar problems 
One of the best parts of this event was being able to explore how developers learn new technologies and work through challenges.  
AI is increasingly becoming an early step in that process. 
Developers are using AI to research unfamiliar topics, understand existing code, troubleshoot problems, and explore possible approaches before deciding what to try next. 
But they aren’t relying on AI alone. 
They still move between documentation, technical videos, sample code, and hands-on experimentation to develop a deeper understanding of what they’re building. And a significant number of participants shared that hands-on learning was a preferred way to learn. 
That stood out to me. 
Even as developers adopt AI-assisted workflows, they continue to value opportunities to work directly with technology, test ideas, and understand how things behave. AI may help developers get started faster. Experimentation helps them decide what to do with what they’ve learned. 
The suite of benefits offered through a Visual Studio Subscription complements this developer journey, not only by providing significant discounts at VSLive! events, but also through access to learning paths, Azure credits, certifications, and hands-on labs.  
More generated code means more to evaluate 
Another interesting observation was how AI is changing the work that happens after code is written. Developers told us AI helps them produce code faster, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’re spending less time on development. 
Instead, they’re spending more time reviewing and validating generated code. Does it work as expected? Does it fit the architecture? Is it secure? Can someone maintain it later? 
These questions have always mattered. AI-assisted development makes them even more important as developers evaluate code they may not have written themselves. 
AI can accelerate development, but developer resourcing and judgment remains essential. 
Time is still the biggest obstacle to learning 
With so many learning resources available, you might expect developers to struggle with finding the right information. But our conversations with developers at VSLive! San Diego signaled that the biggest barriers to learning new skills are time and the pace of technological change. 
Sometimes developers need a quick explanation to move forward. Other times, they need a course, a technical session, a community, or an environment where they can experiment. 
That helps explain why the flexible learning environment at VSlive! matters now more than ever. And it’s another reason Visual Studio Subscription benefits remain valuable. They aren’t just about the software developers use today. They can also help support the technologies and skills developers want to explore next. 
Let’s keep the conversation going 
What stood out most from San Diego was the combination of experience and curiosity. We met developers who have used Visual Studio for decades and are actively exploring how AI can change the way they build software. 
They’re adopting new tools, reconsidering familiar workflows, and looking for more opportunities to experiment. And they’re helping us better understand what developers need as those workflows continue to evolve. 
That’s why the conversations we have at events like VSLive! matter. They give us a chance to hear directly from the people using our tools and help us better understand where we can improve. 
If you’d like to continue learning and connecting with the developer community, join us at future VSLive! events: 
Orlando November 15–20, 2026  
Las Vegas March 22–26, 2027 
Austin May 2–6, 2027 
Thanks to everyone who joined us in San Diego, and especially those who shared their experiences and ideas. The tools developers use are evolving quickly. Hearing how developers are adapting helps us understand what we should build and improve next.

posts.title: 데이터 곤조
posts.author: 강명훈
posts.content:
데이터는 쉽사리 곁을 내주지 않는다. 지저분한 데이터 정리 작업 시작.


엑셀 데이터 필터 기능으로 작업 결과 검증.


한 번으로 끝나는 일은 거의 없다. 2단계.


쓰레기가 줄어드는 게 보이니 기운이 난다(..) 3단계.


4단계에 걸친, 데이터만큼이나 지저분한 정리 작업 완료. 이것도 무수한 삽질 끝에 익숙해진 결과.


10여 년 이상 이런 작업을 해왔으니 익숙해질 만도 하건만, 현실은 매번 어렵다. 데이터 성격이나 목적에 따라 작업 기준이 달라지기 때문. 네가 이기나, 내가 이기나 보자는 승부 근성 or 끝을 보겠다는 똥고집을 부려야 그나마 버티기 수월해진다.


깜짝 놀랄 만큼의 금전 보상이 없는 한, 데이터에 대한 관심과 적성 없이 데이터를 장악하려는 곤조는 발휘되지 않는다. 지저분하고, 단순하지도 않은 작업이 지겹게 반복되니까.
데이터로 온갖 지저분한 가공과 관찰을 하는 동안 데이터의 질감을 느끼게 된다. 자신이 적용하는 모델의 안으로 들어가서 온갖 변형, 시행착오를 거치는 동안 해당 기법에 대한 통찰이 생기게 된다. 반복을 통해 그런 모든 과정에 편안해지는 단계가 있다. 장악의 느낌과 관계 있다... 빙산은 10%만 물 위로 머리를 내밀고 90%는 수면 하에 잠겨있다. 머리를 내민 우아한 작업의 이면에 잠겨있는 잡일이 본질로 보면 더 ‘우아한’ 것일 수도 있다.

posts.creator: 어떤오후의 프리웨어 이야기
posts.title: 스미싱·피싱 문자, AI에게 3초 만에 판별받는 법 (복사해 쓰는 사기 감별 프롬프트 5가지)
posts.author: 어떤오후의 프리웨어 이야기
posts.content:
"고객님 택배 주소가 불일치합니다", "모바일 청첩장이 도착했습니다", "과태료 미납 안내". 하루에도 몇 통씩 들어오는 이런 문자, 진짜인지 가짜인지 헷갈릴 때가 많습니다. 이럴 때 링크를 누르기 전에 문자 내용만 AI 챗봇에게 보여 주면 사기 가능성과 의심 포인트를 바로 정리해 줍니다. 이 글에서는 AI로 스미싱 문자를 판별하는 방법과 복사해서 바로 쓰는 프롬프트 5가지, 그리고 이미 링크를 눌렀을 때의 대응 순서까지 정리했습니다.

이 글의 핵심 요약
1. 링크는 절대 누르지 말고, 문자 텍스트만 복사해서 AI에게 보여 줍니다.
2. 내 이름, 전화번호, 계좌 같은 개인정보는 가린 뒤 입력합니다.
3. AI 판단은 참고용이고, 최종 확인은 공식 앱이나 대표번호로 직접 합니다.
4. 이미 눌렀다면 네트워크 차단, 앱 삭제, 금융사 지급정지 요청 순서로 빠르게 대응합니다.

1. 요즘 많이 오는 스미싱 문자 유형

스미싱은 문자(SMS)와 피싱(Phishing)을 합친 말로, 문자 속 링크를 누르게 해서 악성 앱을 설치하거나 개인정보, 금융정보를 빼내는 수법입니다. 유형은 계속 바뀌지만 뼈대는 비슷합니다.

유형 대표 문구 예시 노리는 것
택배·배송 주소 불일치로 배송이 보류되었습니다 링크 클릭, 악성 앱 설치
경조사 모바일 청첩장, 부고장이 도착했습니다 링크 클릭, 연락처 탈취
공공기관 사칭 과태료·범칙금 미납, 건강검진 결과 확인 개인정보 입력, 결제 유도
지원금·환급 정부지원금 대상자, 세금 환급 신청 신분증, 계좌 정보 입력
가족·지인 사칭 엄마 나 폰 액정 깨져서 이 번호로 연락해 송금, 신분증 사진, 원격 앱 설치
결제 승인 해외 결제 승인 완료, 본인 아니면 연락 바람 가짜 고객센터 전화 연결

 

2. AI에게 묻기 전에 알아 둘 3가지 원칙

  • 링크는 열지 않는다: "확인만 해 보려고" 여는 순간 위험할 수 있습니다. AI에게도 링크 주소를 텍스트로만 보여 주세요.
  • 개인정보는 가린다: 문자에 내 이름, 주소, 일부 카드번호가 들어 있다면 [이름], [카드] 처럼 바꿔서 입력합니다.
  • AI는 실시간 검증기가 아니다: AI는 문구 패턴과 주소 형태로 위험도를 추정할 뿐, 해당 링크가 지금 안전한지 확인해 주지는 못합니다. 최종 확인은 공식 앱이나 대표번호로 합니다.

3. 복사해 쓰는 스미싱 판별 프롬프트 5가지

프롬프트 1. 기본 판별

아래는 내가 받은 문자야. 링크는 누르지 않았어. 이 문자가 스미싱이나 피싱일 가능성을 상, 중, 하로 평가하고, 그렇게 판단한 근거(발신 번호 형태, 문구, 링크 주소, 요구하는 행동)를 항목별로 설명해 줘. 진짜 문자일 가능성이 있다면 공식 경로로 확인하는 방법도 알려 줘.
[문자 내용 붙여 넣기]

프롬프트 2. 링크 주소만 분석

문자에 들어 있던 링크 주소를 텍스트로만 보여 줄게. 접속하지 말고 주소 형태만 분석해 줘. 공식 도메인과 철자가 비슷한 가짜 주소인지, 단축 URL인지, 앱 설치 파일(apk)로 연결될 가능성이 있는지 설명해 줘. 주소: [링크 주소를 띄어쓰기 섞어서 붙여 넣기]

링크가 자동으로 눌리지 않도록 주소 중간에 띄어쓰기를 넣어 붙여 넣는 것도 좋은 습관입니다.

프롬프트 3. 가족 사칭 메시지 대응

가족이라고 하면서 "휴대폰이 고장 나서 새 번호로 연락한다"는 메시지를 받았어. 내용은 아래와 같아. 사칭 가능성을 평가해 주고, 상대가 진짜 가족인지 확인할 수 있는 질문 3개와, 송금이나 신분증 요청을 정중하게 거절하는 답장 문구를 만들어 줘.
[메시지 내용]

프롬프트 4. 이미 링크를 눌렀을 때

방금 의심스러운 문자의 링크를 눌렀어. 내가 한 행동은 [링크만 열었다 / 앱을 설치했다 / 개인정보나 카드 정보를 입력했다]이고, 휴대폰은 [안드로이드/아이폰]이야. 지금 당장 해야 할 일을 시간 순서대로 체크리스트로 만들어 주고, 연락해야 할 기관과 확인할 항목도 함께 알려 줘.

프롬프트 5. 부모님께 설명하기

70대 부모님께 스미싱 문자를 구별하는 방법을 설명하려고 해. 어려운 용어 없이, 카카오톡으로 보내기 좋은 길이로 5줄 이내의 안내문을 만들어 줘. 핵심은 "링크 누르지 않기, 돈 얘기 나오면 전화로 확인하기, 모르는 앱 설치하지 않기"야.

4. AI 없이도 바로 보이는 위험 신호

  • 급하게 재촉한다: "오늘까지", "즉시 확인하지 않으면" 같은 표현으로 생각할 시간을 빼앗습니다.
  • 개인 휴대폰 번호나 해외 번호로 온 공공기관 안내: 기관 안내 문자는 대부분 정해진 대표번호로 옵니다.
  • 단축 URL이나 처음 보는 주소: 공식 도메인과 한두 글자만 다른 주소가 많습니다.
  • 앱 설치나 원격 제어 앱을 요구한다: 정상적인 택배사나 은행은 문자 링크로 앱 설치를 요구하지 않습니다.
  • 신분증 사진, 비밀번호, 인증번호를 요구한다: 어떤 기관도 문자나 메신저로 이런 정보를 요구하지 않습니다.

5. 이미 눌렀다면: 피해 최소화 순서

순서 할 일 방법
1 네트워크 차단 비행기 모드를 켜서 추가 정보 유출을 막습니다
2 의심 앱 삭제 최근 설치한 모르는 앱을 지우고, 휴대폰 백신이나 경찰청 '시티즌코난' 앱으로 검사합니다
3 금융 피해 차단 송금했거나 금융정보를 입력했다면 즉시 112 또는 해당 금융사 고객센터에 지급정지를 요청합니다
4 명의도용 예방 엠세이퍼(msafer.or.kr)에서 휴대폰 가입 현황을 조회하고 가입 제한 서비스를 신청합니다

6. 자주 묻는 질문 (FAQ)

Q1. 링크를 열기만 하고 아무것도 입력하지 않았는데 괜찮을까요?

링크만 열었다면 피해가 없을 가능성이 높지만, 자동으로 앱 설치 파일이 내려받아졌을 수도 있습니다. 다운로드 폴더와 최근 설치된 앱을 확인하고, 백신 앱으로 검사해 두세요.

Q2. AI가 "안전해 보인다"고 하면 링크를 눌러도 되나요?

권하지 않습니다. AI는 문구 패턴으로 추정할 뿐 링크의 실제 상태를 확인하지 못합니다. 택배라면 택배사 공식 앱에서 송장번호로, 기관 안내라면 공식 홈페이지나 대표번호로 직접 확인하는 것이 가장 안전합니다.

Q3. 무료 챗봇으로도 판별이 되나요?

네. 이 글의 프롬프트는 문자 텍스트만 넣는 방식이라 챗GPT, 제미나이, 클로드 등 대부분의 무료 챗봇에서 쓸 수 있습니다.

Q4. 부모님 휴대폰은 어떻게 보호하면 좋을까요?

모르는 출처 앱 설치를 막는 설정을 유지하고, 통신사 스팸 차단 서비스를 켜 두세요. 무엇보다 "돈, 신분증, 앱 설치 이야기가 나오면 일단 가족에게 전화"라는 규칙을 정해 두는 것이 효과적입니다.

마무리: 누르기 전에 3초만 AI에게 물어보세요

스미싱은 기술보다 심리를 노리는 범죄입니다. 급하게 만드는 문자일수록 한 번 멈추고, 텍스트만 복사해서 AI에게 물어보세요. 오늘 소개한 프롬프트 5개를 메모장이나 휴대폰 메모에 저장해 두면, 다음에 수상한 문자가 왔을 때 3초 만에 판단의 실마리를 얻을 수 있습니다.

모르는 출처 앱 설치를 막는 설정을 유지하고, 통신사 스팸 차단 서비스를 켜 두세요. 무엇보다 "돈, 신분증, 앱 설치 이야기가 나오면 일단 가족에게 전화"라는 규칙을 정해 두는 것이 효과적입니다.
마무리: 누르기 전에 3초만 AI에게 물어보세요
스미싱은 기술보다 심리를 노리는 범죄입니다. 급하게 만드는 문자일수록 한 번 멈추고, 텍스트만 복사해서 AI에게 물어보세요. 오늘 소개한 프롬프트 5개를 메모장이나 휴대폰 메모에 저장해 두면, 다음에 수상한 문자가 왔을 때 3초 만에 판단의 실마리를 얻을 수 있습니다.
